findings.field: refutation §2 / advocate.preemptive / sources[0].label — "Vol. II ch. 9, printed p. 137"
findings.problem: The "we are back to geocentrism in any case" passage is on printed p. 138 of the cited OCR, not p. 137. In the archive.org djvu text (item galileo-was-wrong-the-church-was-right-sungenis-vol-1-3-complete) the printed page number sits at the FOOT of its page, so the body between marker "137" and marker "138" is page 138. Three independent anchors fix that convention: the book's ToC puts ch. 1 at p. 11 (marker "10" precedes the chapter opening) and ch. 2 at p. 125 (marker "124" precedes it), and our own already-verified R12 citation of "camouflaged by the term 'cosmological principle'" at p. 309 falls before marker "309". The entry applies that same convention correctly everywhere else — pp. 265, 265-268, 310 and 311 all check out — so this is an isolated off-by-one, not a systematic offset. It matters because this is the "demonstrated" quotation, the single piece of text that answers the advocate's strongest move (the modal distinction between "proves" and "is consistent with"), and the preemptive instructs future editors to keep all three quotations in the body by page number.
findings.fix: Change "printed p. 137" to "printed p. 138" in all three places (refutation section 2, advocate.preemptive, and the first sources[] label), and in docstring note 7. Surrounding text on p. 138: the paragraph runs from "when Einstein's field equations are employed to calculate the forces" to "the proverbial dog chasing its tail", immediately above the "Bondi's Geocentrism" subhead.

findings.field: tldr ("voids the other 458 items on the same list") and refutation §1 ("apply it evenly and the other 458 items go with it")
findings.problem: The quantifier outruns the body and contradicts two later sections of the same refutation. Section 6 states that frame arguments are arguments about states of motion, that shape is neither a state of motion nor a choice of coordinates, and that items 293 and 310 are therefore "inert" on a list whose headline is that the Earth is flat. By the entry's own reasoning an underdetermination claim about the Earth's motion cannot dissolve the list's flat-shape items: the dataset has 54 of them in family B ("Horizon flat in long-distance views", "Bridges no curvature allowance", "Undersea cables straight"). Section 3 makes it worse: it endorses Bouw's route — physics is silent, so choose on theological grounds — as "the consistent party here", which is precisely the position that preserves family C's 69 scriptural items ("Psalm 93:1 immovable world", "Joshua 10:13 sun stood still") intact. So at least 123 of the 458, plus much of family D's historical and philosophical material, survive item 293 untouched. The precise-sounding number is what makes it checkable and wrong, and it is the first sentence a reader meets.
findings.fix: Scope the solvent to what it actually dissolves. TLDR: "...which, taken seriously, voids every item on the list that offers a measurement as proof of the Earth's rest — starting with the two experiments it opens with." Section 1: replace "apply it evenly and the other 458 items go with it" with "apply it evenly and every item on the list that rests on a measurement of the Earth's motion goes with it — beginning with items 1 and 2". Leave the consistent-position sentence that follows, which then reads correctly against section 3.

findings.field: refutation §4, closing sentence ("'No falsifier distinguishing frames' is not a philosophical position; it is a claim about the contents of the literature, and the literature has the falsifiers in it")
findings.problem: Read against the entry's own first paragraph this is self-undercutting. Paragraph one concedes that "no experiment picks out an absolute state of motion", and the compression block establishes that "frames" is the list's swap for Ellis's "models" — a frame is a state of motion, a model is a distribution of matter over hundreds of megaparsecs. Goodman, Caldwell & Stebbins, Uzan/Clarkson/Ellis and Clarkson/Bassett/Lu constrain the matter distribution; none of them distinguishes frames. So on the item's literal words the claim is one we have already granted, and section 4 quotes those literal words before declaring them false. This is the cheapest available counter for a defender — "you conceded it on page one" — and it is available precisely because the sentence drops the reading that makes the section work.
findings.fix: Reattach the reading in the same sentence: "On the only reading that makes it a claim about observations — Ellis's, the cosmological one — 'no falsifier' is not a philosophical position but a claim about the contents of the literature, and the literature has the falsifiers in it, some of them written by the man being quoted. On the frame reading it is true, conceded above, and evidence for nothing."

findings.field: passage.gloss, paragraph 2 ("Read to the end of the paragraph")
findings.problem: The paragraph instructs the reader not to trim Ellis and then stops one sentence short of where the book's block quotation actually ends. In the OCR the quotation runs: "...In my view there is absolutely nothing wrong in that. What I want to bring into the open is the fact that we are using philosophical criteria in choosing our models. A lot of cosmology tries to hide that." The gloss quotes the first two of those and omits the third — which is the sharpest line in the passage and the one most useful to the other side. This is the second clause of the hedge rule pointed at us: a defender who opens the book will find that the sentence we left out is the one that says mainstream cosmology conceals its philosophical criteria, under a heading of ours that told him to read to the end.
findings.fix: Add the final sentence to the same quotation: "...he wants it in the open that 'we are using philosophical criteria in choosing our models. A lot of cosmology tries to hide that.' He is arguing for candour about method, and the complaint in that last sentence is one this page has no interest in softening — it is why the concessions above are stated in his words rather than summarised in ours."

findings.field: clusters.py R11 originator="Gerardus Bouw", originator_work="Geocentricity", year="1992" — rendered beside passage.gloss, paragraph 5
findings.problem: The cluster line publishes a named originator and dated work in the summary row read by people who never expand the entry, while the gloss directly beneath it says the 1992 printing "was not reachable from here and nothing is claimed about its contents", that Bouw credits the claim upstream to Hoyle 1975 and Mach, that ARG-R03 records it in van der Kamp's hands in 1968, and that the located passage "is an ancestor ... and is not evidence of origination". Under the project's own three-state rule an attribution that will not verify is withdrawn to untraced rather than published as fact; here it is published as fact and disclaimed one line later. The treatment reports this correctly and cannot fix it from its own file, which is the "recorded, NOT ACTUALLY APPLIED" pattern curmudgeon.md calls the highest-leverage item on its list.
findings.fix: Not fixable inside _b11_R11.py. In clusters.py, anchored on the "R11" key and never on the originator= line: set originator=None, originator_work=None, year=None and record the repopularisers instead, on the C02 model; keep the existing note, which is separately verified (the genealogy doc sources Bouw's equivalence concession to Faulkner, Journal of Creation 15(2), 2001). Then rewrite the gloss paragraph in the past tense as a completed correction. Until that lands, the page ships a contradiction between the chip and the gloss.

findings.field: refutation §2 and §4 — the book's own p. 311, one page after the passage we quote
findings.problem: A free strengthening is left on the table, and it is one page from a page the entry already cites. Immediately after the Ellis interview quotation the book prints Ellis saying the opposite of what it wants him to say: "there is a preferred rest frame and time coordinate in standard cosmology, and using any other coordinates simply obscures what is happening. The Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation determines the preferred rest frame (and associated time coordinate) to high accuracy" (printed p. 311, verified in the OCR). That is the source itself printing an observationally determined preferred frame on the page after quoting Ellis on undisprovability — a sharper instance of the self-contradiction than the 45-page gap in section 2, and it also pre-empts the defender's "you are inventing the contradiction out of your own cluster assignments". At present the entry uses p. 311 only for the "ironically, moving at the speed of light" jab in straw_man.
findings.fix: Add two sentences to section 2 after the p. 265 / p. 310 pairing: "And the contradiction does not need forty-five pages. On the very next page the book quotes Ellis again, this time saying that in standard cosmology 'there is a preferred rest frame and time coordinate' and that 'the Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation determines the preferred rest frame ... to high accuracy' (ch. 3, printed p. 311). A frame fixed by measurement, to high accuracy, printed one page after the sentence offered as proof that measurement cannot fix one."

findings.field: refutation §4 — "Clarkson, Bassett and Lu published a general consistency test of the Copernican principle in the same volume"
findings.problem: It is not the same volume, and our own sources[] list says so. Caldwell & Stebbins and Uzan/Clarkson/Ellis are Phys. Rev. Lett. 100 (191302 and 191303); Clarkson, Bassett & Lu is Phys. Rev. Lett. 101:011301, confirmed against Crossref. The body therefore contradicts the entry's own citation block on a checkable point, in the section the preemptive identifies as the one a defender will test hardest.
findings.fix: Replace "in the same volume" with "in the same year (PRL 101:011301)".

findings.field: refutation §5 — "the inhomogeneous reading of the supernova data comes 'conceivably with a contribution to the CBR dipole from this inhomogeneity if we are a bit off-centre'"
findings.problem: The parenthetical is attached to the wrong dataset. In arXiv:astro-ph/0602280 it closes the sentence about the number-count/redshift data — "an alternative interpretation would be that this data is evidence of spatial inhomogeneity, i.e. that we live in a spherically symmetric inhomogeneous universe where we are situated somewhere near the centre, with the cosmological redshift being partly gravitational, cf. [71] (and conceivably with a contribution to the CBR dipole from this inhomogeneity if we are a bit off-centre)" — and the supernova sentence is the NEXT one, opening "Similarly the supernova data ... could also be interpreted in this way". The point being made (Ellis allows us to be off-centre) survives intact; only the attribution of the parenthetical is wrong. Same slip in docstring note 8.
findings.fix: "And his 2006 discussion allows us to be off it: on the inhomogeneous reading of the redshift data we live 'somewhere near the centre', 'and conceivably with a contribution to the CBR dipole from this inhomogeneity if we are a bit off-centre' — a reading he then extends to the supernova data in the next sentence."

findings.field: straw_man.detail — "The same passage handles the frame concept loosely enough to describe Ellis's preferred cosmic rest frame as one that is 'ironically, moving at the speed of light' (ch. 3, printed p. 311)"
findings.problem: "The same passage" refers back to the book's Introduction, quoted two sentences earlier (verified at printed p. 1). The "moving at the speed of light" line is 310 pages away in ch. 3. The parenthetical locator saves a careful reader, but the sentence as written attributes to the Introduction something not in it — the exact error class this project treats as its most serious, in miniature.
findings.fix: "The same book handles the frame concept loosely enough to describe..." — or, better, "Elsewhere the same authors handle the frame concept loosely enough to describe...".

findings.problem: The entry's designated load-bearing claim is technically wrong. It says: "a shell drags its interior uniformly, producing no difference between two satellites at different heights, while the signal Ciufolini and Pavlis extract is precisely the 1/a3 difference between LAGEOS and LAGEOS II", and the advocate block declares this "the only part of the frame-dragging argument that survives the relabelling defence". The Ciufolini-Pavlis observable is not a difference and does not isolate a gradient. Iorio (gr-qc/0412057) Eq. (4) states it verbatim: delta-Omega-dot(LAGEOS) + c1 x delta-Omega-dot(LAGEOS II) = mu_LT x S_LT, with c1 = +0.546 and S_LT = 48.1 mas/yr — a positive-weighted SUM (31 + 0.546 x 31.5 = 48.2), obtained by writing Eq. (5) for both satellites and solving a two-equation system in two unknowns, mu_LT and J2. The combination was "built up in order to cancel out the first even zonal harmonic J2", Iorio's words, not to cancel a constant. A spatially uniform interior dragging Omega_c contributes Omega_c(1 + c1) = 1.546 Omega_c to that observable and is absorbed into mu_LT; with two node rates and one nuisance parameter there is no degree of freedom left to separate a constant from a 1/a3 term.
findings.fix: Replace the functional-form claim with the version that is true and still does the work: (a) general relativity predicts the value of the combination, 48.1 mas/yr, with NO free parameter, from the Earth's independently measured polar moment C and spin rate Omega, whereas a uniform cosmic-drag account has to fit a free constant to the same number; and (b) the 1/a3 scaling is tested by adding a node at a different semimajor axis — LARES, a = 7820 km, predicted Lense-Thirring rate about 118 mas/yr — not by the two LAGEOS satellites alone. Then rewrite the advocate.preemptive paragraph, which currently instructs future editors to protect the incorrect sentence.

findings.problem: Chapter 10 of Vol. I is mischaracterised, and the passages where the source does claim a centre are never met. The entry writes that no metric with a preferred central body "is written down in ch. 10 of Vol. I, which argues instead from the existence of the homogeneous solutions", the tldr says "the rotating solutions this argument leans on fix a direction and not a place", and compression.note says the source's weakness is that "the solutions cited are homogeneous or cylindrically symmetric". In the 2006 scan, ch. 10 "Mathematical Models of a Geocentric Universe" is eleven consecutive shell-dragging sections (Hoyle 594, Einstein 607, Thirring 611, Rosser 616, Bondi 619, Brill and Cohen 623, Moon and Spencer 623, Moller 624, Brown 625, Nightingale 625, Lynden-Bell 626, Barbour and Bertotti 628); the only homogeneous-cosmology material in it is the single Obukhov footnote at p. 608 that the entry itself cites. Worse, the chapter asserts a distinguished centre twice. At p. 623 it quotes Brill and Cohen — "in such a model there cannot be a rotation of the local inertial frame in the center relative to the large masses in the universe" — and concludes "either the shell of 'fixed stars' must be fixed around a rotating center, or the center must be the fixed point for a revolving shell". At ch. 12 p. 711 Bennett adds Barbour and Bertotti: "An object at the center of the hollow sphere will not be affected by the inertial forces. The space around the Earth will exhibit the inertial effects of the distant sphere, but not the Earth itself, if it is centrally located." Cylindrically symmetric solutions the source never cites are answered; the centre claim the source does make is not quoted anywhere in the entry. The Maitra/Wright material also comes from OUR Obukhov 2000 review, not from the source.
findings.fix: Rewrite section 1's framing: say the chapter argues from rotating-SHELL results rather than from rotating cosmologies, quote the Brill and Cohen sentence at p. 623 and the Barbour and Bertotti sentence at p. 711, and answer them — the centre of a shell is distinguished by the shell and not by any body sitting in it; the centrifugal term vanishes along the whole rotation axis, a line, not at a single point; and in the complete-dragging limit "no rotation of the local inertial frame in the center" is the statement that the interior co-rotates, which is the relabelling the entry already concedes two sections later. Keep the homogeneity point for the Obukhov footnote, scoped to it.

findings.field: sources[] (Vol. II entry) / refutation (section 2, light cylinder) / people[]
findings.problem: Misattributed location and author. The sources list says the 2013 Vol. II "ch. 10 carries the Godel material inside the fuller Obukhov quotation", and the refutation says "The book meets this head-on in its 2013 volume" before quoting "sauce for the general relativity goose is sauce for the geocentric gander". In the Vol. II scan, Vol. II ch. 10 is "Technical and Summary Analysis of Geocentrism". The Obukhov quotation, the Godel references (Obukhov's "Since the first studies of Lanczos, Gamow and Godel"; Novello/Svaiter/Guimaraes, "Synchronized Frames for Godel's Universe") and the sauce/goose sentence are all on printed p. 647, inside Appendix 1 — "Philosophical and Scientific Ruminations of Martin Selbrede ... As Written in the 1994 Paper 'Geocentricity's Critics Refuse to do Their Homework'". So the superluminal-rotation reply the entry answers is Martin Selbrede's, written in 1994 and reprinted as an appendix, not Sungenis and Bennett's ch. 10 text. Selbrede is separately thanked in Vol. I's front matter for "expertise and consultations". people[] lists only PER-SUNGENIS. On a page whose product is provenance, this is the wrong class of error to carry.
findings.fix: Change the sources line to "Appendix 1, 'Philosophical and Scientific Ruminations of Martin Selbrede', at printed p. 647, carrying the fuller Obukhov quotation, the Godel references and the goose/gander reply". In the refutation, attribute the reply to Selbrede's 1994 paper as reprinted in the 2013 Vol. II rather than to "the book". Note upward that the reply has an author the People tab does not carry. Note also that the 2006 Vol. I answers the superluminal objection in its own voice two pages later, at pp. 615-616, via Rosser — worth citing as the source-side version.

findings.field: clusters.py R05 note and real_source (renders into this entry)
findings.problem: The published page will contradict itself. build.py maps the cluster note to `basis`, and render.py prints `basis` under the verdict chip AND as the summary line of "3 - Refutation". findings.problem: Wrong number. "The claimed balance is out by a factor of about 760, and at the Sun's distance by about 4 x 10^7." The Moon figure is right (757.7). The Sun figure is wrong by three orders of magnitude: on the entry's own constants, omega^2 r at 1 AU = 795.5 m/s2 against GM(Earth)/r2 = 1.781e-8 m/s2, a ratio of 4.47e10. Nothing plausible reproduces 4e7 — using the Sun's own GM instead gives 1.34e5. The docstring's reproduced arithmetic (note 7) contains only the Moon computation, so this figure was added in prose without being computed. It understates our own case, but it is published arithmetic on a page that invites readers to check it.
findings.fix: "and at the Sun's distance by about 4 x 10^10" — or drop the second figure and state the scaling instead, since the mismatch grows as r^3.

findings.problem: The tldr ends on the entry's most contestable move without the qualifier the body insists on. Its closing clause is "setting the Earth's spin to zero makes the prediction exactly zero". The body concedes, correctly and in its own voice, that a well-read geocentrist replies that J is angular momentum relative to the local compass of inertia, that the compass is dragged by the sky in his model, and that "the prediction is unchanged" - "That is correct, and it should be conceded in plain sight." The advocate block rates that same objection as the defender's second-strongest move at survives=4. Readers who never expand the entry carry away the unqualified version, which is the recurring failure the curmudgeon file records for A09, A07, R04, D04 and C08.
findings.fix: End the tldr on what survives the relabelling rather than on the zero. E.g. "...and the defence that rescues it - that the sky drags the compass instead - concedes the Earth turning at one revolution a sidereal day relative to the local inertial compass, measured from orbit to about one part in a hundred."

findings.problem: Unscoped absence claim, in a field the ratchet test does not read. "Nobody in the Lense-Thirring literature makes that claim" is an assertion about an entire corpus made from a sample. tests/test_provenance.py scans tldr, refutation, untraceable, passage.gloss, compression.note and the cluster note; straw_man.detail is not in _blocks, so this passes green - which is exactly the batch-8 finding that the banned construction migrates into unscanned fields. It also sits awkwardly beside our own tldr, which draws an inference of precisely the shape the chapter pre-empts.
findings.fix: Scope it to the texts actually read: "That inference is not made in the papers the chapter itself cites: in Lense and Thirring 1918, in Ciufolini and Pavlis 2004 and in Everitt et al. 2011 the Earth's rotation is an INPUT to the prediction, entering as J = C x Omega, and the measurement tests general relativity given it."

findings.problem: The entry miscounts its own search. "a search of that scan's full OCR text for every plausible spelling of the name returns three hits, two on the incompleteness theorem and one a bibliography line for a biography of Einstein." Re-running that search on the Vol. I OCR returns three hits, but only ONE is on the incompleteness theorem (ch. 5, p. 278). The other two are both Yourgrau's A World Without Time: The Forgotten Legacy of Godel and Einstein - once in a footnote about Einstein's family life, once in the bibliography. The conclusion (Godel's rotating solution is not located in that chapter) is unaffected, but the evidence line is the part a defender will re-run.
findings.fix: "...returns three hits: one on the incompleteness theorem, and two citing Yourgrau's biography of Godel and Einstein - a footnote and its bibliography entry."

findings.problem: The cited URL does not reach the cited text. https://archive.org/stream/GallileoWasWrong/Galileo%20Was%20Wrong_djvu.txt redirects to the item's theater view and contains zero occurrences of "Thirring"; the OCR file in that item is named "Gallileo was wrong_djvu.txt" (double l, lower-case w). findings.problem: Page slip inside the mechanism paragraph. The gloss says a mechanism "follows" the p. 615 sentence and includes "the residual of the rim's motion reaching the Earth is identified with the roughly 4 km/s". In the scan that sentence is on p. 614, BEFORE "We maintain, however...": "Each of the interferometers found a small positive result, coinciding with an ether drift of about 4 km/sec. If this can be attributed to the rotation of the universe wherein the 4 km/sec is the residual drift of that which is much greater at the rim...". The characterisation is fair - the book hedges with "if" and then states it flatly in the next sentence - but the entry's own docstring insists on saying which text is which every time.
findings.fix: "...and, a page earlier at p. 614, the residual of the rim's motion reaching the Earth identified with the roughly 4 km/s the early interferometer experiments were read as showing - offered conditionally and then asserted in the sentence that follows."

findings.problem: A superlative the entry's own source list contradicts. "The most permissive rotating cosmology anyone is currently defending in the literature is around 10^15 times too slow for this argument" rests on Szigeti et al.'s omega_0 = 0.029 H0. The entry's own sources list records Obukhov's 2000 review at "omega/H of order 0.1 at the outside", and section 5.D of that review does adopt omega_t/H_t = 0.1 - three times more permissive. The order of magnitude is unchanged; the superlative is checkable against a source we ourselves cite.
findings.fix: "Even the most rotation-friendly figures in this literature - Obukhov's 2000 review works at omega/H = 0.1, and the 2025 Hubble-tension proposal at about 0.03 - are 10^14 to 10^15 times too slow for this argument."

findings.problem: The section headed "The dates are predicted, years out, in a heliocentric frame" opens "This is where the argument is decided, because prediction is the one thing a coordinate relabelling cannot manufacture" and closes "Every one of those predictions is an assertion about where the Earth will be, and how fast, on a given night. They are not compatible with the Earth being somewhere else." §5 (line 230) then states the opposite in our own voice: a Tychonic arrangement "reproduces every radiant, every closing speed, every apex asymmetry and every annual date, because it is the same geometry with the labels moved" — i.e. the relabelling DOES manufacture the predictions, and under it the Earth is not anywhere else, it is fixed, and the predictions still land. compression.note repeats the concession ("no meteor observation discriminates"). The entry's own advocate.preemptive forbids exactly this move, and build.py strips the advocate block from the published corpus, so the instruction is invisible to readers while the violated sentence is not. This is the defender's first move and our advocate names it in the first line of best_defense.
findings.fix: Replace line 204 with a claim the page can keep: "This is where the model earns its keep, because a prediction registered in advance is a test the bookkeeping can fail." Replace line 212 with: "Every one of those predictions is an assertion about the geometry of an encounter — where the Earth and the stream will be relative to each other, and how fast, on a given night. That geometry is what a relabelling preserves and what a wrong model gets wrong; the predictions test the geometry, not the choice of origin, and section 5 says which of those the list needs."

findings.problem: "the observed peak, radiant, rate and width in general agreement with the models". The rate did not agree with the cited predictions and our own docstring note 5 says so in terms: "It reached only ~1/50 of storm level (Ye & Vaubaillon 2022) — quote the timing, not the rate." Ye & Vaubaillon (cited in our sources) state "Increased activity of the τ-Herculid meteor shower has been observed on 2022 May 30–31 but only reached ~1/50 of storm level"; Egal et al. (also cited) report a peak ZHR of about 27 against predictions of a possible storm, and record that the main peak required ejection speeds four times the typical cometary value. "Width" is not supported by anything in the two cited papers either. A defender holding Ye & Vaubaillon can show our own source contradicting our own sentence.
findings.fix: Replace the clause with: "The outburst arrived in the early hours of 31 May 2022, within minutes of the 2001 and 2008 timings, though at a fraction of the rate the same models had allowed for — Ye and Vaubaillon put the activity at about a fiftieth of storm level. The timing is the part that was booked in advance and cashed."

findings.field: sources[] label for Spurný et al. (line 419); same implication in refutation §2 (line 209)
findings.problem: The source label reads "Asher & Clube, QJRAS 34:481 (1993), whose predicted encounter years 1995, 1998, 2005 and 2008 were confirmed by Asher & Izumi, MNRAS 297:23 (1998)". A 1998 paper cannot confirm encounters in 2005 and 2008. Spurný et al., which we cite for this chain, says something different and checkable: "Asher & Clube (1993) predicted that future encounters would occur in 1995, 1998, 2005, and 2008" and, separately, "Asher & Izumi (1998) showed that enhanced Taurid activity indeed occurred in the years when the center of the swarm was less than 40° in mean anomaly from the Earth" — a retrospective test against historical records, not a confirmation of the four forward years. Line 209 ("Asher and Izumi showed in 1998 that the enhancements had fallen in the years the model named") carries the same implication by adjacency. This is the same overclaim our own docstring note 5 warns about for 2015, made in a different place.
findings.fix: Sources label: "...inside the 7:2 Jupiter resonance proposed by Asher & Clube, QJRAS 34:481 (1993), who predicted encounters in 1995, 1998, 2005 and 2008; Asher & Izumi, MNRAS 297:23 (1998) showed that historical enhancements had fallen in the years the same swarm criterion picks out." Body line 209: "...predicted enhanced encounters in 1995, 1998, 2005 and 2008; Asher and Izumi tested the criterion backwards in 1998 and found the historical enhancements sitting in the years it names."

findings.field: refutation §1 (line 200) and sources[] label for Wiegert et al. (line 424)
findings.problem: "returned in December 2011 with a zenithal hourly rate near 50, from a radiant displaced from the classical one" — and the source label repeats "from a displaced radiant". Wiegert, Brown, Weryk & Wong (AJ 145:70, 2013), the paper we cite, says the opposite about the word "classical": "The radiant at RA +18° and Dec +56° is typical of the 'classical' Andromedids of the early 1800's." What the 2011 radiant is displaced FROM is the 1872/1885 storm radiant at RA +27°, Dec +44°. Our sentence therefore reports the cited paper as saying the reverse of what it says, in the same breath as the storm dates we take from it. The underlying point — the radiant moved relative to the storms — survives intact, which is why this is a one-clause fix rather than an argument problem.
findings.fix: Body: "...returned in December 2011 with a zenithal hourly rate near 50, from a radiant some 9° in right ascension and 12° in declination away from the 1872/1885 storm radiant — back where the 'classical' Andromedids of the early 1800s were — the whole shift reproduced by integrating dust released at 3D/Biela's 1649 perihelion passage." Source label: "...a December 2011 return at ZHR ≈ 50 from a radiant displaced from the 1872/1885 storm radiant and matching the 'classical' early-1800s one, modelled from dust released at 3D/Biela's 1649 perihelion passage."

findings.problem: "a shower with no calendar history at all". Egal et al., which we cite two lines later, states the contrary: "We find that ordinary cometary activity could have produced other TAH apparitions observed in the past, including in 1930 and 2017." The τ-Herculids are IAU shower #61 with a catalogued annual activity period. The true and stronger claim is about the 1995 material, not about the shower.
findings.fix: "...its date fixed twenty-one years in advance by where two orbits would intersect — and fixed for material that did not exist as a stream before the 1995 break-up, whatever the shower's own thin history of apparitions in 1930 and 2017."

findings.problem: The 22% pole-over-equator figure is transplanted across populations. Robertson et al. findings.problem: The diurnal-aberration point is asserted rather than argued, and by the page's own logic in the same paragraph it does not obviously survive: if "radiants and speeds are relative quantities" and a moving-sky model relabels the Earth's 29.8 km/s, it relabels the observer's ~0.4 km/s rotational term the same way — the measured relative velocity is unchanged and the correction is equally required in either picture. The preemptive locks this in as one of three things that "may not be softened", so a defender who spots it in one sentence knocks over a load-bearing third of the closing paragraph. A sky that turns instead would have to impose that same 0.4 km/s on every meteoroid already inside the atmosphere, latitude by latitude and hour by hour, and nothing in the moving-sky picture supplies a mechanism that does it." findings.problem: "The same resonance shows up in diurnal Earth tides recorded by superconducting gravimeters — instruments in basements, weighing the local pull of gravity, with no astronomical input at all." That is false about the method actually cited, and it is the exact overclaim our own advocate/preemptive forbids. Rosat & Lambert (2009), which I read in full (hal.science/hal-00643157/file/11489.pdf), invert complex tidal gravimetric factors for the diurnal lunisolar waves (Ψ1, Φ1 are named as the ones closest to the resonance), computed with ETERNA against an astronomically derived tidal potential and corrected for ocean loading with FES2004 — the forcing, the wave frequencies and the reference amplitudes are all astronomical. The −430-day figure is a celestial-frame period converted from a nearly-diurnal terrestrial-frame resonance using the Earth's rotation rate, so it is not innocent of the assumption at issue either. Our advocate's move 2 attacks precisely this ("agreement between two analyses that share that theory and its tidal model") and our preemptive answers "never write that the gravimeters independently confirm the core" — yet the very next sentence of the published body writes that the resonance is "independently visible in a gravimeter in Germany". The safe version sits in review/advocate.json, which build.py strips from the published data; the unsafe version is what renders.
findings.fix: Replace with: "…recorded by superconducting gravimeters — instruments in basements that weigh the local pull of gravity and never observe a star, though the resonance is extracted from the lunisolar diurnal tides and so is not free of astronomical modelling." Then narrow the closing sentence to the load-bearing claim the preemptive already identified: the resonance is parameterised by the core–mantle boundary flattening, so a moving-heavens account has to explain why the sky is tuned to the Earth's interior. Also correct "a gravimeter in Germany": the paper inverts 15 GGP stations worldwide (Boulder, Bad-Homburg, Cantley, Canberra, Esashi, Matsushiro, Moxa, Membach, Medicina, Metsähovi, Potsdam, Strasbourg, Vienna, Wettzell, Wuhan) expressly "to minimize local effects" — the true version is stronger than the invented specific.

findings.field: refutation §2, passage.gloss, sources[12].label — printed page numbers in Galileo Was Wrong 7th ed.

findings.field: passage.gloss, paragraph 2 ("The claim is a circularity charge…")
findings.problem: "The conclusion is stated flatly and without qualification, and there is no hedge here to shelter behind" is immediately followed by the quotation that refutes it: "Without this methodology, all VLBI measurements are invalid to prove whether the Earth is rotating." The sentence opens with an express condition. A defender's cheapest reply is to point at our own block quote. Worse, the qualification is the best thing in the passage for us and we are throwing it away: the antecedent is the multi-source methodology, which is standard practice and has been since 1979, so on the source's own terms the conclusion never triggers. The hedge rule's whole subject is representing a source's strength accurately, and this is the one place in the entry where we get it wrong — in the source's favour rhetorically, against our own interest argumentatively.
findings.fix: "The conclusion is stated as fact rather than as a possibility, and it is general — 'all VLBI measurements' — but it carries one condition, and the condition is the entry's opening: 'Without this methodology, all VLBI measurements are invalid to prove whether the Earth is rotating.' The methodology in question is ordinary geodetic practice, so the antecedent fails and the conclusion lapses on the book's own terms."

findings.problem: "…but the objection's factual premises fail, including the one about poor resolution". The bare plural reads as universal, and the body's first move is a concession that one of the objection's factual premises is correct: the Tōhoku figures really were computed rather than measured, and JPL's own release says the computed change is smaller than the accuracy with which the length of day can be measured. The TLDR erases the concession that is the refutation's strongest credibility move and asserts a quantifier the body denies in its opening paragraph. This is recurring failure #2/#6 exactly.
findings.fix: "…but the objection's premises about the instrument fail — the single source, the poor resolution, the unchanged historical record — including the one about resolution: …". That keeps the punch, matches §7's own enumeration, and leaves the conceded premise standing where the body puts it.

findings.field: passage.gloss, paragraph 6 ("An internal tension worth knowing about")
findings.problem: "…and thereby states the principle — resolution goes as wavelength divided by baseline — that makes the ch. 2 objection wrong." The book states no such principle there. I read the whole "On Telescope Limits" section in the OCR (leaf 1055): the words baseline, wavelength and aperture do not occur in it. It says only that point sources closer than the angular resolution cannot be resolved, that a single optical telescope does worse than one arcsecond in practice, that "the highest angular resolutions can be achieved by interferometry", and gives VLTI 0.001″ and Hubble 0.05″. Both examples are optical, so a defender reconciles the two chapters in one line — "we said radio wavelengths give poor resolution; the VLTI is an optical instrument, there is no contradiction" — and our claimed tension evaporates. The real tension is narrower and survives that reply: ch. 2 treats resolution as a function of wavelength alone, while ch. 10 concedes that interferometry, not aperture, sets the achievable resolution.
findings.fix: "…gives the Very Large Telescope Interferometer's target of 0.001 arcseconds and Hubble's 0.05 arcseconds — conceding that it is interferometry rather than aperture size that sets the achievable resolution, which is the variable the ch. 2 objection leaves out. (Both of the book's examples are optical; the physics that closes the gap for radio is in section 3 below.)"

findings.problem: "The imputed reasoning — that a belief in rotation is what makes the shortcut seem acceptable — is supplied by the paragraph, not by anything in the analysts' documentation." That is an unscoped absence claim about an entire corpus (NASA/JPL/IVS/IERS documentation) that nothing in this entry records having searched. straw_man.detail is reader-facing (render.py line 242) but is NOT one of the six fields the ratchet in tests/test_provenance.py scans (tldr, refutation, untraceable, passage.gloss, compression.note, cluster note), so the counter stays green — this is literally the batch-8 finding that the construction migrates into unscanned fields, one batch later.
findings.fix: "…is supplied by the paragraph; it is not stated in the description of the analysis the frame is actually built from (Charlot et al. 2020, Sects. 2–3), which is the document searched for this entry."

findings.problem: The quotation "excellent agreement with the independent measurements by VLBI" could not be verified in any accessible copy. Schreiber et al., PRL 107:173904 (2011) is closed access (OpenAlex reports no repository full text anywhere; APS returns 403; no arXiv version located). Crossref confirms title, five authors, volume and article number, and the PubMed abstract confirms the 16 m² helium-neon ring laser, the Wettzell affiliation and direct detection of the Chandler and annual wobble — but it says the detection "is verified by comparing the time series of the ring laser measurements against the 'C04 series' of Earth rotation data from the International Earth Rotation and Reference System Service." IERS C04 polar motion is a multi-technique combination in which GNSS, not VLBI, dominates. So both the quoted phrase and the sentence built on it — "reproduces polar motion derived from quasars" — rest on text I cannot reach and may misdescribe the comparison series. The flicker-floor figure and the Apr–Jul 2010 window are unverified for the same reason.
findings.fix: Either cite the page of the PRL where that phrase appears, or fall back to what the abstract carries: "…detected the Chandler and annual wobbles directly, verified against the IERS C04 Earth-rotation series." And soften "polar motion derived from quasars" to "the same polar motion the space-geodetic services measure", unless the VLBI-specific comparison can be confirmed in the paper.

findings.problem: "…and ICRF3 pins source positions to a noise floor of 0.03." No unit, immediately after a figure quoted in arcseconds. Milliarcseconds is meant; read as arcseconds it is off by a factor of 1,000 and inverts the comparison.
findings.fix: "…to a noise floor of 0.03 mas."

findings.problem: "the technical chapters are Bennett's" is asserted as fact. No statement of chapter-by-chapter authorship is located in the 5.5 MB OCR text searched for this entry; the book is credited jointly to Sungenis and Bennett throughout. The claim is charitable in effect — it explains the ch. 2 / ch. 10 tension as co-authorship rather than bad faith — but it is an unsourced attribution about a named living co-author, which is the class of claim this project polices hardest.
findings.fix: "Different chapters, different volumes, and a two-author book; this is offered as a tension in the text, not as an accusation." Drop the authorship attribution unless a statement of it can be located and cited.

findings.problem: "An assumption cannot be confirmed at 25σ by the residuals of the analysis that supposedly assumed it" closes a paragraph about Gaia. The 25σ is ICRF3's radio detection (5.83 ± 0.23 µas/yr); Gaia's own significance is 5.05 ± 0.35, about 14σ. The preceding clause names ICRF3, so a careful reader is safe, but a skimmer takes 25σ as Gaia's number, and this is the entry's closing line on the circularity charge.
findings.fix: "An assumption cannot be measured at 25σ in the radio and independently at 14σ in the optical by the residuals of the analyses that supposedly assumed it."

findings.field: untraceable (Sargent paragraph) + sources[Flat Earth Society interview]
findings.problem: The Flat Earth Society interview we cite and quote does contain the word we say is not located in it. Sargent: "But on a flat earth model, well it could also be density. I think its electromagnetic. I think its a molecular magnet that pulls things down." That is about gravity, not the dome, so our sentence — "an electromagnetic, toroidal or resonance description of IT is not located in either" — is narrowly true. But it is the single best quote-mine available against this entry, in a source we link, and a defender needs one sentence to make the page look like it searched carelessly. Worse for a provenance review: this is the strongest proximate lead for item 201's exact phrasing. A distributor reading this one page meets "an enclosed system with a dome over it" and "I think its electromagnetic" four paragraphs apart, and "Firmament as electromagnetic dome." is what that fusion would look like. We found the lead, read past it, and published the negative.
findings.fix: Add to the Sargent paragraph, before "The video series itself was not reached": "One qualification, because a reader who opens the interview will find it. Sargent does use the word electromagnetic there — but of the downward pull, not of the dome: asked about gravity he answers “I think its electromagnetic. I think its a molecular magnet that pulls things down.” The dome, a few paragraphs earlier, is Genesis 1:6 and the planetarium. So the two nouns of item 201 are both on that page and the sentence joining them is not — which is a lead we record rather than a source we can credit." Stating it strengthens the untraced finding instead of leaving it as a hole; do not withdraw the untraced verdict on the strength of it.

findings.problem: The entry's own advocate rates the 10.59-versus-7.83 gap as the defender's strongest move (move two, survives=4) and preemptive (a) requires that we state it in our own voice up front. The refutation does. The two fields that render BEFORE it do not. The TLDR says "Schumann derived the mode ladder in 1952 from a sphere of radius 6,371 km, and Balser and Wagner measured it from 1960" — derived, then measured, with nothing between them; and steelman.why says "A prediction made from an assumed shape, before the measurement, is the strongest evidence about shape that this phenomenon can carry, and it did not come out flat." As stated, that prediction failed by 26%. A reader meets the unqualified prediction-then-measurement story twice (tldr first of all, steelman as section 2) before meeting "the absolute number does not settle anything" in section 3. That is the TLDR outrunning the body, and the steelman outrunning it in the same direction.
findings.fix: TLDR, replace the middle sentence with: "Schumann derived the mode ladder in 1952 from a sphere of radius 6,371 km, and Balser and Wagner measured it from 1960 — the ideal formula overshoots the fundamental by a quarter, for a known reason, but the ratios between the modes, which contain no cavity size at all, come out spherical to a few per cent." In steelman.why, after "strongest evidence about shape that this phenomenon can carry", insert "— and it is the mode ratios that carry it, not the absolute frequency, which the ideal formula misses by 26% for reasons set out below —" before "and it did not come out flat."

findings.field: refutation §1 (final sentence of the 7.83 paragraph) — with clusters.py D17
findings.problem: Two coupled defects. (a) clusters.py D17 still carries note="…the number only comes out right on a globe" and originator="Mark Sargent"/originator_work="Flat Earth Clues"/year="2015". render.py sets basis = cluster note, and the basis renders twice — under the verdict chip and as the summary line of the Refutation section — while the meta line renders "first published by Mark Sargent" directly above a block headed "No original to quote / This cluster has no named author and no traceable source publication." findings.fix: Land the clusters.py edit first, anchored on the "D17" key and not on the byte-identical originator= line: originator/originator_work/year → None, and note → "Sargent's enclosed-world model is real but is not the source of these three items. The Schumann resonance is derived from the Earth-ionosphere cavity treated as a *sphere* of radius 6371 km; the ideal formula misses the observed 7.83 Hz by 26%, and the load sits on the mode ratios, which contain no cavity size." findings.problem: The range does not reproduce from the two ladders printed three lines above it, under either convention. Disc 1, 1.59, 2.14, 2.30, 2.65 against observed 1, 1.80, 2.59, 3.36, 4.15 gives deficits of 11.7%, 17.4%, 31.5%, 36.1% relative to observed, or excesses of 13.2%, 21.0%, 46.1%, 56.6% relative to the disc. findings.field: tldr and verdict_challenge.reasoning (item 202, technical reading only)
findings.problem: advocate.preemptive (d) states the rule for this entry: both readings of "toroidal", technical first and iron-filings second, "because answering only the technical one is the straw man the defender is accusing us of". findings.fix: In verdict_challenge.reasoning, after "not detectible at the surface", add: "and on the looser reading the item is more likely to intend — the iron-filings doughnut — the same thing happens one level down: that field is described by the IGRF as a spherical-harmonic expansion and generated in a spherical convecting outer core mapped by seismology, so the geometry is inside the citation on either reading." In the TLDR, "the toroidal part of the field is the part confined to the core and not measurable at the surface at all" → "the toroidal part of the field is the part confined to the core and not measurable at the surface at all — and the part a compass does feel is mapped, since Gauss, as a spherical harmonic series."

findings.field: passage.gloss ("Neither cosmological lineage brought this argument in.") and docstring note 4a
findings.problem: The searches are named, then the conclusion generalises from three texts — two of them single editions, one a single volume of three — to two entire lineages. Zetetic covers Rowbotham, Carpenter, Blount, Voliva, Johnson, Dubay; Tychonian covers Sungenis, Bouw, van der Kamp, Marshall Hall. This is failure pattern #1 in the exact form the batch-8 sweep predicted: it passes the ratchet regex in tests/test_provenance.py ("Neither … brought" matches none of the _ABSENCE patterns) while violating the rule the regex exists to enforce. The docstring commits it more baldly — "The founding flat-earth texts have no astrology argument in them." The sentence is load-bearing: "It came off the esoteric shelf" rests on it.

findings.problem: Leg 2 of the proposed verdict change is overstated on two counts, and the entry tells the operator "Either leg alone carries the verdict." (i) It is not attribution-free as claimed ("it needs no attribution at all, only two clusters of the same list"): its punchline clause — "and that occultist is a heliocentrist" — is precisely an attribution to Hall, the thing the entry elsewhere and rightly says is not established. (ii) Worse, a well-informed defender turns the leg round: D10's thesis is that heliocentrism has occult roots, so an occultist who puts the sun at the centre is *evidence for* D10, not a contradiction of it. The residual tension is rhetorical (calling a witness you impugn elsewhere), not logical. That reply is the single strongest available against the proposed verdict and it appears nowhere in advocate.best_defense, which rates itself 4 on four other moves.
findings.fix: Downgrade leg 2 in verdict_challenge to a supporting observation: strike "Either leg alone carries the verdict" and "it needs no attribution at all", and add the defender's reply to advocate.best_defense as a fifth move with an answer — that D09's items are occult-symbolic material regardless of who wrote them, so the list is still using as evidence the tradition it convicts, but that this is a rhetorical inconsistency and the verdict rests on leg 1.

findings.problem: Three prevalence claims, none sourced: TLDR "most charts cast today are computed from JPL's solar-system integration"; body "the usual computational basis for astrological software"; steelman "what most astrological software has run on for a quarter of a century". I re-read the cited Astrodienst page for a market-share statement and there is none on it — it describes the toolset and the DE lineage, not adoption. A quantifier in the TLDR with no support is exactly recurring failure #2/#6, and the project's own sourcing standard is that every claim cites a public source or a reproducible calculation.
findings.fix: Either cite something that supports the prevalence (Astrodienst's licensee list, or a named set of packages that ship SE), or reword to what is documented: "the ephemeris that Astrodienst distributes for astrological software, and whose three data options are the JPL DE files, Astrodienst's compression of them, or Moshier's semi-analytic fit to them — all three JPL-derived." That version needs no market claim at all and makes the same point.

findings.problem: The answer to the defender's first move reads: "Hall's opinion settles nothing about the sky, which is why sections 2, 3 and 4 do not mention him." Section 3 names Hall at least six times and is built on his text — "Hall's own definition", "Hall's 23° 28′", "Hall's own gloss on it", "The plate at the head of his zodiac chapter", "Hall knows what kind of object it is and says so", "Hall's twelve gates", "Hall himself has to note". The substantive defence survives (section 3 uses Hall as the source of the claim under analysis, not as an authority on the sky) but the sentence certifying it is false about our own body, and advocate.preemptive is the artifact that discharges a survives=4 rating. Not reader-facing — render.py does not emit the advocate block.
findings.fix: "…which is why sections 2 and 4 do not mention him at all, and section 3 cites him only for his own definition of the zodiac — as the text being analysed, never as an authority on the sky."

findings.problem: "applying light-time and annual aberration, a 20.49″ correction whose whole content is the earth's orbital velocity divided by the speed of light" overstates what is applied. 20.49552″ is the *constant* of aberration, i.e. the maximum; the displacement actually applied is κ·sin θ with θ the angle from the apex of the earth's motion, so for chart bodies it runs from near zero to 20.5″. As written, the sentence is false for some positions on any given chart — in the paragraph we bill as "the cleanest single object in the argument" and mark "Recomputed here 2026-08-10", which is where a technically literate astrologer will look first.
findings.fix: "…applying light-time and annual aberration, a correction of up to 20.49″ whose scale is set by the earth's orbital velocity divided by the speed of light (the displacement is the constant times the sine of the angle from the apex of the earth's motion, so it varies across the chart and vanishes nowhere the argument needs it to)".

findings.problem: We paraphrase Hall as saying "the only trouble with heliocentric astrology is that it is comparatively new". Hall wrote "The great difficulty, however, with the heliocentric system is that, being comparatively new, there has not been sufficient time to experiment successfully and catalogue the effects of its various aspects and relationships." "The great difficulty" is not "the only trouble" — a paraphrase that strengthens a source's concession in our favour, which is the drift this project exists to catch, committed on our side. The stated reason for paraphrasing rather than quoting is also now weaker than it looks: the OCR reads "there has not been sufficient timetoexperimentsuccessfullyandcataloguetheeffects of its various aspects and relationships", which is recoverable by respacing, and the second witness we already cite carries the sentence.
findings.fix: Quote it: "The great difficulty, however, with the heliocentric system is that, being comparatively new, there has not been sufficient time to experiment successfully and catalogue the effects of its various aspects and relationships" — noting the word spacing is collapsed in the scan and was restored against the sacred-texts transcription. Then "Not wrong. Young." lands on Hall's own words.

findings.problem: Two small problems with the weakest link the entry itself identifies. (i) The gloss says "the argument below does not lean on it", but the plate is the closing beat of the item-199 paragraph in the refutation ("the thing at the centre of the zodiacal circle is not the earth at all but 'the fiery altar of Divinity'") and again in the compression note. It leans. (ii) Its placement is asserted twice as "at the head of his zodiac chapter" / "the plate facing the zodiac chapter"; the chapter opens at LIII, and the one index line I could find for this plate appears to read "Facing LI" — and the caption is absent from both the sacred-texts pages for the zodiac chapter (sta12) and the preceding chapter (sta11). The caption text itself I did verify verbatim in the archive OCR.
findings.fix: Either drop the plate from the item-199 paragraph and let "imaginary celestial angles" carry it — the argument survives intact — or keep it and scope the placement: "the zodiacal-egg plate, which the 1945 scan places near the opening of this chapter (Hall's index appears to give 'Facing LI'; the caption is not located in the sacred-texts transcription of either chapter)".

findings.problem: The quote is truncated mid-sentence, without a trailing ellipsis, at the exact clause that reverses its force. Both scans read: "As it stands, there was a lot of room to make adjustments to Ptolemy's model to fit the observations, but no one was willing to do so ONCE COPERNICUS' SYSTEM WAS SEIZED AND PROMOTED BY THE RENAISSANCE AND ENLIGHTENMENT AS A MEANS TO DEMOTE THE AUTHORITY OF SCRIPTURE AND TAKE CONTROL AWAY FROM THE CATHOLIC CHURCH TO INFLUENCE THE MINDS OF MEN." We stop at "do so", present the remnant as a concession in the book's own voice (gloss: "the adjustments... were never made"; refutation section 2: "the book's own next move is to say the note was never redeemed"), and then answer the deleted clause in the TLDR ("The model was not put down by decree") without ever showing the reader that the source states it. The seventh edition sharpens the same claim two lines earlier: "Copernicus... chose not to make those adjustments and instead wanted to throw the baby out with the bath water." This is the hedge rule violated on our side, in the field the reader treats as the source's own words, on a page whose entire premise is that truncation is the offence.
findings.fix: Mark the truncation and disclose the rest. The 57-word quote is at the 60-word cap, so trim the first sentence to "before Kepler's improvements to the heliocentric model, Copernicus' system was no more accurate than Ptolemy's" and end the second with "...but no one was willing to do so ..." with a visible ellipsis; then add one gloss sentence: "The sentence does not end there. It continues 'once Copernicus' system was seized and promoted by the Renaissance and Enlightenment as a means to demote the authority of Scripture' - so this is not a concession that the model failed but a claim that it was abandoned for non-scientific reasons, and that claim is what the chronology below answers."

findings.problem: "the source makes it carefully - quoting Owen Gingerich and Arthur Koestler rather than asserting it" is contradicted by our own compression block, which quotes the same claim "in the book's own voice", and by the verified text at printed p. 211 of both editions, where the book asserts it flatly ("Copernicus' system was no more accurate than Ptolemy's") and immediately goes beyond it with an unhedged counterfactual the historians do not support: "if Ptolemy's model had been properly adjusted, it would have shown as much accuracy as the best heliocentric model." The headline sentence therefore both misdescribes the source and is stronger in the source's favour than the body it summarises.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The claim is true, and the source states it at about the right strength - asserting the parity in its own voice and backing it with Owen Gingerich and Arthur Koestler rather than with the movement's own authorities: before Kepler, Ptolemaic tables really were about as good as Copernican ones."

findings.problem: The TLDR's flagship example of the model being "overturned in steps" is the Moon whose disc should nearly double, and the closing paragraph lists "the lunar diameter that would not double" first among the measurements that superseded the model. That measurement does not discriminate geocentrism from heliocentrism at all: the Moon orbits the Earth in every system, the defect is in Ptolemy's lunar sub-model, and it was repaired INSIDE geocentric astronomy by Ibn al-Shatir - a fact section 2 supplies itself ("it is why Ibn al-Shatir and later Copernicus rebuilt the lunar model"). The least discriminating item on the page is in its most prominent position, on an entry whose verdict is precisely that the cluster does not discriminate.
findings.fix: In the TLDR, replace "starting with a Moon that its own parameters require to nearly double in apparent size against an observed variation of 14 per cent" with "ending with aberration and parallax, the one class of measurement the source's own authority concedes the geocentric case cannot absorb." Keep the Moon in section 2 but add its boundary there: "This is a defect in Ptolemy's lunar model, not in geocentrism - Ibn al-Shatir repaired it without moving the Earth. It shows the model was corrigible by measurement, which is the point; it does not by itself decide where the Earth is."

findings.problem: "a 301-comparison audit of Alfonsine against Copernican predictions for the 1560s". Tipler and Bollinger's audit does not cover the 1560s; it covers Tycho's observation notebooks from 1 May 1564 to 9 January 1601 - a 37-year span, verified against the article. Compressing it to one decade understates the evidence and misdescribes a cited source in the sentence carrying the entry's strongest institutional support for parity.
findings.fix: "a 301-comparison audit of Alfonsine against Copernican predictions drawn from Tycho's observation notebooks between 1564 and 1601 finds Ptolemy ahead on the inferior planets and the Sun while Copernicus is ahead on the superior ones".

findings.problem: The table is introduced as "his epicycle radii from the Almagest as tabulated by Linton", but its Saturn row uses 6;30, and Linton (From Eudoxus to Einstein, ch. 3, p. 78, verified in the PDF we cite) prints 6;32 - as our own sources label correctly states. So the displayed primary figure is the one number in the table our cited source does not print, and the parenthetical presents Linton's actual value as the variant. A reader who follows the citation to check the flagship computation finds the attribution inverted.
findings.fix: Make Linton's value primary and footnote the Almagest variant: "Saturn 6;32 -> 9.184 (modern 9.5549, -3.9%)", and change the parenthetical to "(...Saturn's epicycle is given as 6;30 in some readings of Almagest XI, which moves it to 9.231 and -3.4%.)" Either way, the sentence introducing the table must not attribute to Linton a number he does not print.

findings.problem: "Bessel measured the parallax of 61 Cygni in 1838 at 0.314" +/- 0.020"" and "Bradley found stellar aberration in 1728" both disagree with the same figures elsewhere on our own site: A05 and deep_batch2 give 0.3136" +/- 0.0136" (313.6 +/- 13.6 mas, which is what the source A05 cites says), and A03 and deep_batch2 date Bradley's discovery to 1729. Neither figure has a supporting entry in this entry's sources block. This is exactly the cross-claim consistency surface a critic assembles into "the site contradicts itself".

findings.problem: "Kuhn moved from 'measurably superior' in 1957 to parity by 1960." Kuhn's 1957 "measurably superior" was said of Reinhold's Prutenic Tables, not of Copernicus's system, and Kuhn 1957 p. 171 already states parity - the very page the source book quotes ("was about as accurate as the heretical suggestion put forward in 1543 by Copernicus", footnoted to Kuhn 1957 p. 171). Presented as a clean reversal, the sentence overstates what Tipler and Bollinger establish and mischaracterises a named historian in one clause.
findings.fix: "Kuhn called Reinhold's Prutenic Tables 'measurably superior' in 1957 while conceding on the same book's p. 171 that Copernicus was about as accurate as Ptolemy, and by 1960 was stating the parity flatly." Apply the same correction to the sources label.

findings.problem: The two quotes used to identify the straw man - "except perhaps a bias against Ptolemy" and "neither drawn to scale nor was ever adjusted for errors" - are the 2006 wording, and the field names no edition. The second phrase returns zero hits in the seventh-edition scan, which reads "neither absolute in its distances nor ever adjusted to make it correct" instead. A reader checking the seventh edition, which the entry's own locator points at, will not find the words we quote.
findings.fix: Insert the edition once: "...the book replies (2006 scan, ch. 4 at printed pp. 210-211; the seventh edition rewords the second phrase) that the textbook diagrams..."

findings.problem: The refutation's closing discriminator paragraph rests on ARG-A03 and links to it, and the compression and steelman both lean on the aberration/parallax combination, but A03 is absent from `related` while A22, R01 and R08 - none of them load-bearing here - are present.

"Inverse-square on those gives brightness swings of 53 against 54. The epicycle reproduces the observed swing to about one per cent." The two numbers just given differ by about 2%, and "observed" is doing unearned work: Mars's actually observed brightness range is far wider than 54x (roughly -2.9 to +1.9 magnitude, a factor near 80) because of phase angle, so a reader who takes "observed swing" to mean observed brightness finds the claim wrong by a factor rather than by one per cent.
findings.fix: "Inverse-square on those gives brightness ratios of 53 and 54. The epicycle reproduces the geometry that drives the variation - the distance ratio - to about one per cent; the brightness actually seen swings wider still, because phase angle adds to distance."

findings.problem: The azimuthal-equidistant circumference is computed for 45°N, not 45°S. On a north-polar AE map the 45°S parallel has radius R×135° = 15,013 km and circumference 94,319 km = 50,928 nmi; the published 31,440 km / 16,975 nmi is 2πR(π/4), the 45°N value. So the sentence "22,000 nautical miles is 30% more than the flat azimuthal-equidistant map predicts for that same parallel, which is 16,975 nmi" is wrong by a factor of three AND reversed in direction — 22,000 nmi is 57% BELOW what the disc requires. The conclusion drawn from it, "too big for the globe and too big for the disc", is false on the second half, and the paragraph is introduced as "the check that settles it". advocate.preemptive repeats the error ("the Victorian sailing distances overshoot the flat map by 30% as well") and rests part of the answer to the defender's strongest move on it.
findings.fix: Replace with the correct computation and keep the point, which gets stronger: on the north-polar AE chart the 45°S parallel measures 94,319 km (50,928 nmi), so Rowbotham's 22,000 nmi is 57% SHORT of what the disc demands while being 44% over the globe's 15,282 nmi. Rewrite the conclusion as: his data fit neither model, overshooting the globe and falling far short of the disc — which is what sailing-route distances compared with arcs of a parallel look like. Fix the same number in advocate.preemptive and in docstring 5(c) so the three agree.

findings.problem: The sign-reversal argument does not discriminate, and on the documented track it favours the source. Under uniformly stretched southern parallels the navigator always over-reckons progress along track, which puts an eastbound ship WEST of its DR and a westbound ship EAST of its DR. Milner's ships were eastbound to India (west of DR); Wilkes's Antarctic cruise was westbound — the Vincennes worked the coast from 140°30′E to 112°16′E toward a westward goal of 105°E (United States Exploring Expedition, Jan–Feb 1840) — so "consistently east of his reckoning" is the SAME along-track error as Milner's and is precisely what Carpenter's and Rowbotham's model predicts. The text asserts the opposite ("Errors that reverse sign … are what local currents look like, not what a rescaled globe looks like") and presents it as "the discriminating detail". It also locates Wilkes in the Drake Passage, which neither Dubay's item nor the expedition record supports for that report.
findings.fix: Delete the sign-reversal claim and replace it with the argument that actually works: a stretched-parallel model predicts a fixed FRACTIONAL over-reckoning that grows monotonically with southern latitude and is identical on every heading and every day, whereas the reported errors are intermittent, vary with locality and season, and reverse relative to heading — the signature of set and drift. If the current line is kept, note that the Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows eastward and so displaces a ship east of DR regardless of heading, which fits Wilkes's report directly; and state Wilkes's actual working ground (Wilkes Land, roughly 100–160°E) rather than the Drake Passage.

findings.problem: The words "consistently east of his reckoning, sometimes over 20 miles in less than 18 hours" are quoted as Wilkes's ("Wilkes recorded being …", "Wilkes's reported 20 miles of unaccounted easting"). They are Dubay's, from 200 Proofs item 37 ("in his journals also mentioned being consistently east of his reckoning…"). The docstring gets the provenance right ("Dubay 37 has Wilkes…"); the published text does not. Wilkes's Narrative was not consulted, so a secondary summary is presented as a primary record and then used as the empirical anchor of both the steelman and the sign argument. On a project whose product is provenance this is the worst available place for it.
findings.fix: Attribute the quotation to Dubay and scope what was checked: "Dubay's proof 37 reports that Wilkes 'mentioned being consistently east of his reckoning, sometimes over 20 miles in less than 18 hours'; the wording is Dubay's and was not located in Wilkes's Narrative of the United States Exploring Expedition, which was not reached for this entry." Then say the argument does not depend on the attribution being right.

findings.field: clusters.py B12 originator (renders as the meta line) vs passage.gloss and people[]

findings.field: steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim ("The measured figure at 45° is 48.99 statute miles"), refutation §2 ("The measured ratio is 1.00"), tldr ("A degree of longitude measures…")
findings.problem: These are values computed from the GRS80 ellipsoid, not measurements. Rowbotham's demand was specifically for "proper geodetical operations" in the far south, and the entry answers it with a formula. The advocate's fourth move names this exactly ("You have not been to 45 degrees south with a chain either… Rowbotham asked for a survey. You have given him a table") and advocate.preemptive answers only that the arithmetic is reproducible — which is not the same as measured. Reproducibility of a model is the weakest available reply to a demand for a survey.
findings.fix: Cite a southern-hemisphere measurement and say the demand was met on its own terms: the 1870s telegraphic longitude determinations along the Australia–Java cable, the Australian geodetic surveys, or modern GNSS/VLBI baselines across Australia, any of which fixes east–west separations in the south directly. Then say the ellipsoid value is what those measurements return, rather than presenting the ellipsoid as the evidence. Adjust advocate.preemptive to point at the measurement rather than at the arithmetic.

findings.problem: preemptive instructs "Keep section 4 labelled as illustration", and section 4 carries no such label — it is headed "The modern version of his experiment, which anybody can run this week" and reads as a primary argument. The whole point of the preemptive is that the §4 numbers DO depend on the azimuthal-equidistant map (the defender's second move: "You have refuted Gleason 1892 and called it a refutation of us"), so a published instruction describing a safeguard that is not in the text is the failure the sweep keeps catching — prose telling a reader something about the page that is not true of it.
findings.fix: Either add the label to §4 — one clause, e.g. "the figures below assume the Gleason-style north-polar chart, and are an illustration; the argument of §1 does not depend on any particular flat map" — or change preemptive to the past tense describing what was actually done. Do not ship the instruction as though it had been followed.

findings.field: compression.note ("The enclosing dome is later furniture, from the 2015 enclosed-world material")
findings.problem: An origin claim with no name and no citation. The docstring says "Sargent-era (2015)", but the published note names nobody and cites nothing, and the entry's own searches found no "dome" in Dubay 2015 either — so the reader is given an unfalsifiable pointer to unspecified 2015 material. On a project whose standing rule is named author, pre-modern, or untraced-rather-than-guessed, this is a guess in the voice of a finding, sitting in the block that publishes our provenance verdict.
findings.fix: Either name and cite the text (Mark Sargent, Flat Earth Clues, 2015, with a locator), or write the honest version: the word "dome" is not located in the three navigation texts searched, and where the specimen's compiler got it was not traced for this entry. findings.problem: Two problems in one paragraph. findings.field: tldr and refutation §8 ("hands off to the spherical sailings after a few hundred miles")
findings.problem: Two separate statements in Bowditch art. 2402 are merged. The manual says plane sailing "provides solution for latitude of the point of arrival, but not for longitude. To calculate the longitude, the spherical sailings are necessary" — unconditional, at any distance — and separately that plane sailing "is not intended for distances of more than a few hundred miles". Our version implies the handoff is distance-triggered. The true fact is stronger than the one published: the flat method cannot do longitude at all, which is the quantity this entire cluster is about.
findings.fix: Split them: "plane sailing cannot give you a longitude at any distance — the manual sends you to the spherical sailings for that — and is not intended for runs of more than a few hundred miles in any case."

findings.problem: "Bowditch's chapter on the sailings classes it among the spherical sailings" — chapter 24 does not classify great-circle sailing that way in so many words. It lists seven sailings without grouping them, calls parallel sailing "the simplest form of spherical sailing", and solves great circles with an oblique spherical triangle. The explicit definition is in the Glossary: "Any of the sailings which considers the spherical or spheroidal shape of the earth is called spherical sailing."
findings.fix: Cite the Glossary for the classification and chapter 24 art. 2406 for the spherical-triangle solution, so the sentence rests on the text that actually says it.

findings.problem: The through-line that 'Constant solar diameter' is Proctor's sentence, borrowed — TLDR: 'the words are a quotation from the astronomer he was arguing against'; §3 heading: 'is Proctor's sentence, borrowed'; compression.note: 'Nothing was misquoted; the speech act moved' — understates Carpenter's own commitment and mislocates the drift. In proof 89 Carpenter asserts the luminous-object law himself first, in his own voice, with his own example ('Sail past the light of a small lamp in a row-boat on a dark night, and it will seem to be no smaller when a mile off than it was when close to it'), and then endorses Proctor's line as true: 'And then he forgets the fact!' — a sentence our own compression.source_wording quotes and the analysis then does not reckon with. So constancy is already a positive datum in the movement's voice inside the source, and proof 89 is already a numbered proof. The speech act moved from Proctor to Carpenter in 1885, not from Carpenter to the list, which makes force_upgraded the wrong reading of this transition. A defender's reply writes itself: 'your headline provenance finding describes our author's rhetoric, not your list's compression.'
findings.fix: Rewrite the first paragraph of compression.note to say that Carpenter states the luminous-object law himself and calls Proctor's admission 'the fact', so what the list compresses is Carpenter's own assertion buttressed by an opponent's concession — and relocate the drift to what the fragment actually does, which is strip the law ('luminous bodies do not shrink with distance') down to a bare astronomical datum about the Sun, i.e. hedge_dropped/scope_widened rather than force_upgraded, or say in the note that the enum has no clean value here as it already does for item 31. In the TLDR replace 'where the words are a quotation from the astronomer he was arguing against' with something like 'where the movement's own luminous-object law is buttressed by a quotation from the astronomer he was arguing against'. Change the §3 heading to '“Constant solar diameter” is a perceptual law, propped up by an opponent's admission'.

findings.problem: 'So the chain from the quoted page above to the item on the list is documented at every link' is not supported. findings.problem: The blockquote splices printed p. 71 and printed p. 120 into one continuous italic block, and marks the ~49-page jump with the same '…' used two clauses earlier for a one-paragraph elision within p. 71.
