findings.problem: 'Winship converts a units error into an unanswerable challenge — "We challenge the whole scientific world to disprove this statement"' attaches that sentence to the wrong claim. In the scan it closes the sun's-DISTANCE argument ('IT IS AS CERTAIN AS THAT TWO AND TWO ARE FOUR, THAT THE SUN'S DISTANCE FROM THE EARTH IS TWO THOUSAND SEVEN HUNDRED NAUTICAL MILES. We challenge the whole scientific world to disprove this statement,'), immediately before the new section headed 'SUN'S DIAMETER.' The units error is the diameter derivation, and its challenge is a different sentence: 'Let him disprove this who can. If ever disproof is attempted, it will be a literary curiosity, well worth framing.' Our own sources[] label already places the 'two and two are four' line with the distance, so the entry contradicts itself on where the quote lives. Also: the same field's 'The objection was arithmetic and the reply was about character' drops the one substantive move in proof 89 — Carpenter's claim that the objection rests on 'the non-appearance of a thing which has never been known to appear at all'.
findings.fix: Swap the quotation to 'Let him disprove this who can. If ever disproof is attempted, it will be a literary curiosity, well worth framing.' And soften the second sentence to something like: 'The reply mixes one empirical claim — that the predicted enlargement has never been observed — with several paragraphs about the objector's character.' The empirical claim is the one §4 answers, so naming it strengthens rather than weakens the section.

findings.problem: 'Rowbotham's third edition of 1881 rewrites the 1865 section and reverses it' overstates what changed, and the defender's comeback is in Rowbotham's own 1865 text. Section 8 of 1865 already carries the whole atmospheric mechanism — 'as the air near the Earth is both more dense and more damp ... the light of the Sun must be dilated or enlarged as well as modified in colour' — and only then adds the Philips micrometer sentence. The 1881 chapter keeps the identical mechanism (its enlarged disc is explicitly 'the disc of light projected upon the atmosphere') and drops the micrometer concession. So a defender can answer: he always said the glare dilates, he never said the micrometer reading changes, and your §6 'contradicted by the very steadiness Carpenter would go on to rely on' therefore lands on a claim he did not make. The file's own docstring §5 warned against exactly this framing ('state it as a comparison of two editions ... not as "Rowbotham contradicted himself"') and the published prose went the other way.
findings.fix: Recast as: 'Both editions carry the same mechanism — damp low air dilating the light. What the 1881 rewrite removes is the concession: the 1865 section closes by quoting Philips that the instrumental measure is identical at horizon and meridian, and chapter X drops that sentence and promotes the residual appearance to "a striking argument against the rotundity of the earth".' That is the true and stronger claim, and it survives the glare-versus-disc reply.

findings.problem: The entry computes that Rowbotham's 700-mile Sun should set at 0.11 of its noon width and then leaves the atmospheric answer to be handled qualitatively in §6. The killer number is one line away from figures already on the page and is never stated: Rowbotham's damp air would have to magnify the setting disc about ninefold — roughly 800% — to hold it at 32'. Stated that way, chapter X stops being a rival explanation and becomes a quantitative commitment nobody has ever measured. As written, a defender gets to treat 'perspective plus atmospheric magnification' as an unpriced alternative.
findings.fix: Append to §4: 'For that Sun to keep its width, the low atmosphere would have to magnify the disc about ninefold. Rowbotham's chapter X claims a magnification but never a magnitude, and no measurement of the horizontal disc has ever shown one — the 1865 edition says so in his own book.'

findings.problem: 'the tradition's founding text' is used twice for Rowbotham 1865. The founding text is the 1849 pamphlet — works.py carries WRK-ROWBOTHAM-1849 and the state doc notes it is public domain and not digitised anywhere reachable; README dates Rowbotham's writing 1849–65. The entry's own sources[] label is careful ('1865 first book edition'), so the page contradicts itself in miniature, and edition dating is one of the four recurring failures.
findings.fix: 'the movement's first book-length statement' or 'Rowbotham's 1865 book' in both places.

findings.problem: Antia et al. state the 5 km figure conditionally — 'If these changes are due to variation in solar radius then the implications are that the solar radius decreases by about 5 km from minimum to maximum activity.' The refutation reports it as what 'helioseismic estimates of the kind reported by Antia and colleagues put any change at', and the source label flattens it further to 'any cycle change is "about 5 km"'. The direction (a decrease with rising activity) is also dropped. The stripping is conservative-safe here — if the conditional fails there is no radius change at all — but §7 exists precisely to model care about a live question, so it is the wrong paragraph to paraphrase loosely in. The label also omits the journal and year (Solar Phys. 192 (2000) 459) that the Rozelot label supplies.
findings.fix: '...report that if the observed f-mode frequency shifts are due to a radius change at all, the implied change is about 5 km between activity minimum and maximum', and add 'Solar Physics 192:459 (2000)' to the label.

findings.problem: The Moon and the Sun are compared on different quantities. 'Widely separated observers see the Moon displaced ... by tens of arcminutes' is a two-observer difference, while 'the Sun's displacement is under nine arcseconds' is the single-observer horizontal parallax; the matching two-observer figure for the Sun is up to about 17.6". The error is in our favour by a factor of two, in a paragraph whose whole point is a clean 390:1 comparison.
findings.fix: '...where the same pair of observers see the Sun shift by under twenty arcseconds' — or keep 8.8" and say 'horizontal parallax' for both bodies rather than mixing the two framings.

findings.problem: 'That is why the Sun and the Moon come out the same size and the same distance in his hands' credits Winship with an equal-distance result he does not compute. The unit rule implies 3,437 nmi for anything measured by it; Winship's own distance comes from the separate 45-degree baseline procedure and is 2,700 nmi — which the very next sentence correctly uses against him. 'Equal size and equal distance' is Dubay's formulation of the output, not Winship's derivation.
findings.fix: 'That is why anything measured by that rule comes back the same size and the same distance — and why Dubay can report the two bodies as "of equal size and equal distance". Winship's own numbers show the seam: ...'

findings.problem: 'the OCR reads "tcund" where the word is plainly "found", and that is the only silent repair in the quote below' is not accurate — the quote also silently repairs the scan's 'the diameter is of couse 32 miles' to 'of course' (a repair independently corroborated by Scott's 1901 reprint, which prints 'of course'). Separately, §1 says the flat 32-mile figure follows the 'if, indeed' hedge 'three paragraphs later'; it is four. Docstring only, so no reader sees it, but quote provenance is the one place this project cannot afford a loose claim about its own accuracy.
findings.fix: '…two silent repairs: "tcund"->"found" and "couse"->"course", the latter confirmed against Scott's 1901 reprint of the same sentence.' And 'four paragraphs later'.

findings.problem: "inside a single British survey the predicted lean between stations is a few arcseconds and is swamped by the local deflections that produced Rowbotham's anomaly" is wrong by three orders of magnitude, and it contradicts the entry's own arithmetic. The stations run Dunnose 50 deg 37' to Clifton 53 deg 27' — 2.839 deg, 316 km — so the two verticals lean by 2.84 deg = 10,221 arcsec. Even the narrowest row, Dunnose-Greenwich, is 3,092 arcsec. By the entry's own d/R formula (42 arcsec over 1,298 m), 316 km gives 10,230 arcsec; a reader who takes section 5 seriously and then reads this sentence has caught us contradicting ourselves inside one entry. The sentence also collapses on itself: a few arcseconds cannot be 'swamped by' local deflections that the same entry puts at 2-5 arcseconds. This renders in the 'The list overstates its own source' section, which is the block the whole project is built to publish.
findings.fix: Replace with the quantity actually meant: "inside a single British survey the two verticals lean by 2.8 degrees and nobody could miss it; what is a few arcseconds is the quantity that DISCRIMINATES plane from globe — 34 m of flattening signal across the table's latitude band, or about 1 arcsec of station latitude — and that is what the 2-5 arcsec local deflections swamp. 'Worldwide' is the scale at which two verticals differ by up to 180 deg and at which bridge towers are built non-parallel on purpose."

findings.problem: "so the ellipsoid's residuals span 257 m where the plane's span 227 m: neither figure of the Earth fits, and the plane fits no better." The 'so ... :' marks this as an inference from the two numbers, and the numbers point the other way — 227 is smaller than 257. Recomputed against WGS84: residual RMS is 98.9 m for the ellipsoid and 84.9 m for a constant-degree (plane) model, because the table's trend runs opposite to the ellipsoid's. On this table, on both range and RMS, the flat model is the better fit. A defender paid to knock this down needs five minutes and a spreadsheet, and the sentence is in the section the file itself calls the centrepiece.
findings.fix: State it the way the numbers do: "On this table a constant degree length actually fits marginally better than the ellipsoid — RMS 85 m against 99 m — because the observed trend runs the wrong way for polar flattening. That is not a result about the Earth; it is a measurement of how far the station errors overwhelm the signal, since the flattening the ellipsoid predicts across this band is 34 m and the scatter is 227 m. What the table does refute is the plane's actual prediction, which is not 'a constant that fits within 227 m' but EXACTLY EQUAL degrees — and the page it stands on shows 0.20 per cent."

findings.problem: The author attribution is wrong. Sensors 16(4):565, 'A Comparative Study of the Applied Methods for Estimating Deflection of the Vertical in Terrestrial Geodetic Measurements', is by Vittuari, Tini, Sarti, Serantoni, Borghi, Negusini and Guillaume (verified via Crossref and Europe PMC, PMC4851079). Riccardo Barzaghi is first author of a DIFFERENT Sensors 2016 paper on deflections of the vertical — 16(8):1168, 'Computing the Deflection of the Vertical for Improving Aerial Surveys: A Comparison between EGM2008 and ITALGEO05 Estimates' — which is exactly the kind of near-miss that gets a site accused of citing from memory. Title, journal, volume, issue, page and URL are all correct, so a reader clicking through lands on a paper whose author list does not contain the name we printed.
findings.fix: "Vittuari et al., 'A Comparative Study of the Applied Methods for Estimating Deflection of the Vertical in Terrestrial Geodetic Measurements', Sensors 16(4):565 (2016)". Same change in the docstring at item 6(c).

findings.problem: "the first two agree well within 1 arcsecond, the gravity-derived values sit about 2.5 arcseconds out" misreads the paper. In Vittuari et al. the 1 arcsec and 2.5 arcsec figures are STANDARD DEVIATIONS, not departures: 'The method that combines leveling and GNSS has slightly larger standard deviations; although well within the 1 arcsec level ... the geoid model based method, whose 2.5 arcsec standard deviations exceed this threshold, is also statistically consistent with the others.' The actual ITALGEO2005 departures from GNSS-LEV in Tables 1-2 are 0.8 and 1.8 arcsec at Medicina and 0.2-0.6 arcsec at Noto. The error runs against us — it manufactures a 2.5 arcsec disagreement, comparable to the whole effect under discussion, in the one paragraph whose job is to say three independent instruments agree.
findings.fix: "the astro-geodetic and GNSS-plus-levelling values differ by 0.4 arcsec and 0.0 arcsec at Medicina, and the gravimetric geoid — quoted by its authors at a 2.5 arcsec standard deviation, the loosest of the three — is statistically consistent with both. Starlight, a levelling staff and a gravimeter, three different physical measurements, return one tilt."

findings.problem: The paragraph quotes McNair's own error estimate — 'an error he put at not more than 0.003 ft' — and then, three sentences later, gives the predicted convergence as 0.0031 ft, without noticing that these are the same number. As printed, our own figures say McNair's stated precision was equal to the effect, which invites the obvious reply: 'by his numbers he was capable of seeing it, and what he saw was 0.141 ft the other way.' The answer exists and is not stated: 0.003 ft was his reading precision, while the 0.028-to-0.141 ft dispersion across shafts, wires and bobs is the real uncertainty — a systematic ten to forty-five times the signal. (Also: 0.141/0.0031 is 45, so 'one fortieth of the largest' understates our own case.)
findings.fix: After the arithmetic, add: "McNair's quoted 0.003 ft is his reading error, and it is the same size as the predicted signal — which is precisely why the experiment settles nothing. What defeated it was not precision but a systematic: his results scattered across 0.169 ft between shafts, wires and bobs, ten to forty-five times the effect being looked for, and he identified the cause himself."

findings.problem: Section 5 rests entirely on design dimensions — 'These are dimensions on drawings, and two structures were built to them' — which leaves the advocate's circularity charge (move 2) unanswered in the one place it is easiest to answer. A defender says: the 1 5/8 inches was CALCULATED from an assumed globe before a rivet was driven, so quoting it back is quoting the assumption. The rebuttal is inside the Humber sentence we already print and never draw out: 'The towers, ALTHOUGH VERTICAL, are 1.4 inches farther apart at the top.' Each tower was set plumb to its own local vertical by instrument; the spread at the top is the observable consequence of the two verticals differing, and it is checkable by construction survey rather than by cosmology.
findings.fix: Add one sentence after the Humber quote: "Note what that sentence concedes about method — each tower is vertical, set plumb to its own local gravity, and the tops come apart anyway. The spread is not a curvature allowance bolted onto a straight structure; it is what two plumb lines 1,410 m apart do, surveyed during construction."

findings.problem: Two small overstatements of the 1911 EB. findings.fix: In section 1 replace with: "the Encyclopaedia Britannica computes deflections for sixteen astronomical stations in that survey — six under 2", six between 2" and 4", four above 4" — and prints per-station values for three of Rowbotham's own: Arbury Hill -3.0", Greenwich -2.5", Clifton Beacon +1.3"." findings.problem: advocate.survives=4 means 'must be answered in the body', and MOVE FOUR's answer is deferred conditionally — 'in the body if this is ever attacked in public'. build.py strips the whole advocate block from the published corpus into review/advocate.json, so the single best sentence in the file ('inference from starlight is what an astronomical latitude has always been, including every latitude in Rowbotham's own table, so a defender who disqualifies it disqualifies the evidence his own argument is made of') is invisible to every reader. findings.field: refutation, section 5 "Their own horizon distances are sqrt(2Rh)" (scripts/_b11_B02.py:308,310; same claim in docstring note 7 at :113)
findings.problem: The 6-ft/3-mile pairing is called "the cleanest single check on this page" and Carpenter's figures are said to BE the sphere's formula. They equally reproduce the zetetic tradition's own law, which Rowbotham states quantitatively at p. 160 of the same enlarged-edition file the entry quotes, citing Mayhew's Wonders of Science p. 357: an object vanishes beyond "3000 times its own diameter". 6 ft x 3000 = 3.4 miles, against the sphere's 3.00 miles and Carpenter's "about three miles" - the two laws (sqrt(2Rh) and 3000h) cross at an eye height of about 1.4 m, so the check is made at the one height where the rival predictions agree. The closing sentence then says the perspective account "has no dependence on the observer's height whatever", which Carpenter contradicts in proof 6 - the proof quoted three lines above - with "if we merely ascend a hill such as Federal Hill, Baltimore, we may see twenty-five miles away", and which Rowbotham contradicts in his stated proposition 2 ("the further any two bodies ... are asunder, the further must they recede before they appear to converge to the same point"), the clause that makes the vanishing distance scale with the eye's height above the plane.
findings.fix: Demote the 3-mile datum and promote the 200-mile one. Replace with: "Proof 32 does not discriminate: six feet at three miles is sqrt(2Rh) to two significant figures, but it is also the zetetic rule Parallax quotes at p. 160 - an object invisible beyond 'three thousand times its own diameter' puts a six-foot object at 3.4 miles - and the two laws cross at about 1.4 m of eye height, which is where Carpenter is standing. Proof 6 is where they part. Their law is linear in height and the sphere's goes as its square root: at the 26,675 ft a 200-mile horizon requires, three thousand diameters gives a horizon some fifteen thousand miles away. Carpenter reports two hundred." Delete "has no dependence on the observer's height whatever" and write instead "makes the range grow in direct proportion to the height, not as its square root"; fix docstring note 7 to match.

findings.field: refutation section 2(a) (:282), steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim first reply (:260), gloss (:251), tldr (:203-204)
findings.problem: Our headline internal-contradiction argument - his optics exempt the axis his own tilt-to-contact procedure uses - is presented as an oversight of his, and the source's printed answer to exactly that charge is nowhere in the refutation or the steelman. In TANGENTIAL HORIZON at p. 202, describing the same procedure we quote, Rowbotham says the dip required to bring cross-hair and horizon together is "the angle A, T, S, to which must be added the collimation", and repeats "always A, T, S, plus collimation"; his reason follows at pp. 203-204, two sentences after the sentence we quote from p. 203: "the spider's web of which the cross hair is made is placed in the actual centre; hence, in an observation, the point absolutely opposite to it is not seen, but only some other point minutely distant from it". The gloss acknowledges the escape route but attributes it to the 1865 text only, so a reader of the edition we quote is told his answer lives somewhere else; the TLDR then states the exemption flat, without the hedge the gloss carries.
findings.fix: In section 2(a), after the exemption quotation, add: "He saw the objection. In the same section he writes that the dip measured this way is the geometric angle 'to which must be added the collimation', because the cross-hair itself occupies the centre, so 'the point absolutely opposite to it is not seen, but only some other point minutely distant from it' (enlarged ed., pp. 202-204). That answer is available to him, and it is why (c) below is written not to depend on (a): whatever residual the spider-line leaves is a fixed property of one instrument." In the gloss, change "He has an answer to this in the 1865 text" to "He has an answer to this in both editions - 1865 puts it as ... and the enlarged edition restates it at pp. 203-204 ...". Soften the TLDR to "the optical defect he describes acts off the axis, and his own procedure puts the horizon on it".

findings.problem: "Rowbotham's own 66 feet, converted at the 10-to-17-mile ranges his text names" attributes a distance range to the source that neither text contains. Experiment 7 names "a length of ten to twenty miles" and "Ten miles on each side"; Dubay proof 60 names "a clear, flat 10-20 miles". Seventeen appears nowhere in either (the only "17 miles" in the enlarged edition is a latitude discrepancy in an Australian survey). Because the angle is proportional to the half-trace, the range the texts do name gives about 2.2 to 4.3 arcminutes, not 2.5 to 4.3. On a page whose subject is what sources actually say, a number in quotation-adjacent position that the source does not carry is the error we exist to catch.
findings.fix: "And Rowbotham's own 66 feet, converted across the ten-to-twenty-mile traces both texts name, is between about 2.2 and 4.3 arcminutes."

findings.problem: "The strongest version of this argument is not in the 1849 pamphlet, which was not reached for this review" asserts an absence and concedes in the same clause that the text was never searched. This is the enforced rule verbatim - unreachable is not absent - and the pamphlet is not a safe bet to wave away: its own title is "A description of several experiments which prove that the surface of the sea is a perfect plane", so sea-horizon experiments are exactly what it advertises. The docstring (note 3) has the honest version, resting on Experiment 15's Brighton buildings postdating 1849 and calling that corroborating rather than decisive; the published sentence dropped the scope.
findings.fix: "The strongest version of this argument is not located in either text read here; the 16-page 1849 pamphlet was not reached for this review and has not been checked for it, though Experiment 15 is sited at buildings that postdate 1849."

findings.field: steelman.why_it_doesnt_save_claim, "It reverses" (:262); same argument in refutation 2(c) (:286)
findings.problem: The reversal test is built on a definition of collimation - "a fixed angular offset between the line of sight and the instrument's mechanical axis" - that is the surveyor's error, not the one our own passage block quotes from the source three screens earlier: "a slight divergence of the rays of light from the axis of the eye, on passing through the several glasses of the theodolite", demonstrated with a magnifying glass and explicitly radial (outward from the centre, zero at the centre). A radially symmetric magnification effect is not obviously face-dependent, so as written the two-face argument answers a different error from the one Parallax proposes, and a defender who has read the lens paragraph will say so. The test does still bite - his residual offset is fixed in the instrument frame, so transiting flips it relative to gravity - but the text never makes that connection.
findings.fix: Add one clause: "His 'collimation' is not the surveyor's line-of-sight offset but a radial divergence through the glasses - yet the test still applies, because on his own account the observed point sits at a fixed small offset from the cross-hair, fixed in the instrument, so transiting the telescope carries it to the other side of the vertical and the two-face mean removes it. The dip does not move, because it is fixed by gravity and geometry."

findings.field: passage.gloss, "The witnesses he calls do not testify for a plane either" (:252)
findings.problem: "A plane does not look like a bowl" is asserted as self-evident against a source that argues the opposite at length on the same pages, and that our own quotation is drawn from. Two paragraphs before the balloon accounts Rowbotham writes that on a plane the sea "appears to rise up on all sides equally and to surround him like the walls of an immense amphitheatre. He seems to be in the centre of a large concavity"; immediately after them he explains the appearance with the tunnel analogy, the surface rising to the line of sight "in the same manner that the ceiling and the floor of a long room ... appear to approach each other". Producing the bowl from a plane by perspective is the whole point of his model, so our one-liner engages nothing and hands a defender the reply.
findings.fix: Replace "A plane does not look like a bowl." with: "He has a theory of why a plane would look like a bowl - the surface rising to the eye-line in every direction, as the floor and ceiling of a long room appear to converge - so these witnesses are not neutral testimony he collected but reports his perspective model was built to accommodate. What they do not report is a plane; what they report is an appearance, and an appearance is the quantity under dispute."

findings.problem: Our headline quote stops one sentence early, and the omitted sentence is the source's answer to the reading our gloss builds on it. In the Vol. II scan the passage continues: "But when the heavens are postulated to be in motion, it is Dr. Nieto's equations that are deficient, not ours." The gloss says the conditional "gives the whole game away"; Selbrede's very next line pre-empts exactly that reading (the conditional is counterfactual in his model, and he turns it into an attack on his critics' equations). On a page whose whole thesis is that trimming a source changes it, a defender gets to say we trimmed his paragraph at the most convenient point. The substance is answered elsewhere in the body (the rotation rate is an input, section 1), but the answer is never attached to the sentence that provokes it.
findings.fix: The 60-word cap blocks extending the quote (47 + 19 = 66). Handle it in the gloss instead, which is our own prose: after "would fall if they stopped", add a clause naming the rejoinder and answering it — e.g. "Selbrede's next sentence turns the concession round — when the heavens are postulated to be in motion, he says, it is his critics' equations that are deficient, not his — and that is fair as far as it goes; the objection here is not that the conditional is false but that the rate of turning it makes everything depend on is an input, read off the rotating-globe solution and put in by hand."

findings.problem: The verification claim is stated more precisely than the book's own citations warrant, and more strongly than the research note allows. The refutation says every paper "exists, at the journal, volume and page range it gives"; the TLDR says "cited at the right journal, volume and pages". Checked against the scans: Grøn and Eriksen is given in full and exactly right (the essay itself, printed p. 632: "General Relativity and Gravitation, Volume 21, No. 2, 1989, pgs. 105-124"); but Orwig carries NO volume number anywhere I could find — Vol. I footnote 1168 and the Vol. I bibliography both read "Physical Review D, 1757-1763, 1978", and the essay names Orwig without a citation at all; Brill and Cohen at Vol. I footnote 1188 reads "Physical Review, 143, Issue 4, March 25, 1966, pp. 1012, 1014" — quote pages, not the article range 1011-1015; Thirring is given as "Physikalische Zeitschrift 19, 33, 1918", a start page rather than a range. Nothing the book prints is wrong, which is the point the paragraph is making and it survives — but we credit it with a bibliographic precision it does not have, and the docstring's own instruction was 'say so, at that strength and no higher'. The TLDR carries the strongest form of it and is what most readers see.
findings.fix: Refutation: "Every bibliographic detail the book prints for them checks out — journal, volume and year — and where it gives a page range (Grøn and Eriksen at 105-124, Orwig at 1757-1763) the range is right; Orwig's volume number the book omits, and the pages it cites inside Brill and Cohen and inside Grøn and Eriksen are quote locations we did not open the papers to confirm." TLDR: "...are real, and every journal, volume and year the book gives for them checks out."

findings.problem: The two texts the renderer puts side by side do not support the label attached to them. render.py prints list_phrasing ("Geostationary satellites fit rotating sky model.") above source_wording ("This motion of the firmament is evidenced ... by geosynchronous satellites ... the satellites would fall to the earth") and then the drift label. Against that pairing the list is not upgraded — it is weaker than the source, which asserts evidential force flatly while the item only says "fit". force_upgraded means a concession or permission re-used as a proof, and the permission that justifies the label is the p. 637 "by definition" thesis, which appears only inside the note. A reader who reads the block as rendered sees a label the visible evidence contradicts, on the project's flagship mechanism.
findings.fix: Put the licensing sentence into the field that renders: source_wording = "'This motion of the firmament is evidenced ... by geosynchronous satellites ...' (p. 648), and, as the essay's thesis: 'it is impossible to launch an attack on geocentricity on the basis of general relativity, by definition' (p. 637)." The note already explains the reasoning and already concedes the enum choice is contestable; this only makes the block's own evidence carry its own label.

findings.problem: The box answers "proof of a moving earth is proof general relativity is a myth" by saying the Earth's rotation relative to the local inertial frames "is measurable, frame-independent, and measured, by ring-laser gyroscopes and by the Foucault pendulum the essay itself discusses", and stops. Read strictly it is true — the relational quantity is agreed by both accounts — but it reads as an evidential claim, and it is deployed two boxes away from a passage in which the source claims the Sagnac effect and Coriolis forces as evidence FOR the firmament's rotation, and a refutation that concedes perfect dragging makes the two descriptions indistinguishable. The defender's reply writes itself: under perfect dragging the compass of inertia turns with the heavens, so that measurement is exactly what we predict too. This is the class of opening the docstring's own section 7 was written to avoid — winning on a point where the defender is right.
findings.fix: Add one clause and close the box on the narrow point it actually needs: "...measured, by ring-laser gyroscopes and by the Foucault pendulum the essay itself discusses. Both accounts predict that measurement and neither can claim it — what is measured is the relative rotation of the ground and the local compass of inertia, and the models differ only over which of the two to call at rest. The point here is narrower: establishing that relative rotation would leave general relativity exactly where it was, so the second sentence's threat is empty."

findings.problem: The passage we quote names three evidences — the Sagnac effect, Coriolis forces, geosynchronous satellites — and the entry silently answers one of the three. A06 (Foucault) and A09 (Coriolis) are cross-linked; A02 (Michelson-Gale / Sagnac interferometry, verdict REFUTED) is not, although Sagnac is the first item in the sentence we put in the passage block. A07 (gyroscopes / ring-laser gyros, verdict SELF-CONTRADICTED) is not linked either, although the straw_man box rests its argument on ring-laser gyroscopes.
findings.fix: related=["A02", "A06", "A07", "A09", "A13", "A18", "A20", "A22", "R01", "R06", "R08"], and one clause in the gloss noting that the sentence's other two evidences are answered at A02 and A09 so a reader does not think we picked the easy third.

findings.problem: Two unscoped universals, both sitting in fields the absence-claim ratchet in tests/test_provenance.py does not read (it scans tldr, refutation, untraceable, passage.gloss, compression.note and the cluster note): "Nothing in the Machian picture supplies any of those three" and "No physicist claims the Earth rotates in the pre-relativistic absolute sense". Both are claims about an entire literature or an entire profession made from a sample, and both are the exact migration the batch-8 sweep described when it concluded that writers learn the regex rather than the rule. The entry knows the rule — it uses the scoped form correctly twice in the refutation — so this is inconsistency rather than ignorance.
findings.fix: "Nothing in the Machian material read for this review supplies any of those three — in Thirring, in Brill and Cohen, in Orwig, or in Grøn and Eriksen the shell's rotation rate is an input, not a result." And: "The claim modern physics makes is not rotation in the pre-relativistic absolute sense the sentence assumes; it is rotation relative to the local inertial frames."

findings.problem: The two longitude figures in the same sentence contradict each other. Equilibria of the equatorial ellipticity term alternate every 90 degrees, so stable points sit 180 degrees apart and 90 degrees from the unstable ones: given unstable points at 165.3E and 14.7W, the stable pair is 75.3E and 104.7W, not 75.3E and 108W. We are faithfully repeating the cited Wikipedia article, which prints 108W, but we print the pair that exposes the inconsistency and a reader who does the arithmetic finds it in a paragraph whose purpose is to show that we do the arithmetic.
findings.fix: Either write "75.3°E and about 105°W" in both the refutation and the source label, or keep 108°W and add "(sources differ between 104.7°W and 108°W for the second stable point)". Same change in the sources[] label so the two agree.

findings.problem: Two internal-note errors that will propagate into record_problems and into whoever picks this up next. (a) The Selbrede essay in the Vol. II scan does not end at printed p. 648 — that is only where the quoted sentence sits. The essay runs to p. 652; Appendix 2 ("Gravitational Lensing: Real or Imagined?") begins at p. 653, and the table of contents gives "Appendix 1: Interview with Martin Selbrede 623". So "printed pp. 630-648" understates the essay by four pages. (b) The header line says the attribution challenge is filed "in record_problems — see 8 below", but section 8 is the verdict discussion; the record defects are section 9 (and the attribution itself is section 1). Neither error reaches the published fields — the sources[] label correctly says "from printed p. 630" with no end page.
findings.fix: Section 2: "Vol. II scan, Appendix 1, printed pp. 630-652: the Selbrede essay (Appendix 1 itself opens at p. 623 with a 2012 documentary interview; Appendix 2 begins at p. 653)." Header: "see 9 below".

findings.problem: The entry names Dubay proof 158 as one of the three modern ancestors of items 108/227, but the body never answers it, and the body's §2 headline superficially confirms it. Proof 158 (verified verbatim in the Internet Archive djvu text) grants co-rotation arguendo and concludes 'Hot-air balloons would also be forced steadily faster Eastwards as they ascended through the ever increasing atmospheric speeds.' Our §2 then presents 'at mid-latitudes it is predominantly eastward' as the fact that points 'the wrong way for the claim'. A well-informed defender replies: 158 predicted eastward sweeping; you have just reported it as observed and called it a refutation. The actual answer exists in the entry but is never connected — §1's angular-momentum result is westward (-4.7 m/s), i.e. the opposite sign to 158's prediction, and in solid-body rotation a rising balloon gains linear speed but no motion relative to the ground beneath it.
findings.fix: Add two sentences to §2 (or the end of §1) naming proof 158: solid-body co-rotation means uniform angular velocity, so a balloon rising 39 km is carried east faster in absolute terms and not at all relative to the ground under it — 158 confuses absolute speed with relative displacement. Then state that the residual that does exist runs westward at 4.7 m/s by angular-momentum conservation, which is the wrong sign for 158, and that the observed eastward drift is thermal-wind, identifiable by its latitude structure and its hemispheric sign reversal rather than by altitude.

findings.problem: The gloss reports proof 22 as 'Baumgartner, after some two and a half hours of ascent over New Mexico, "2500 miles West into the Pacific Ocean"'. Dubay's text reads 'spending 3 hours ascending over New Mexico'. The 2.5 h is the real ascent time (Wikipedia: launch 09:30 MDT, jump 12:07/12:08 MDT), not his. The refutation compounds it: 'Dubay's figure of about 2,500 miles is the equatorial version of that speed (1,039 mph) run for two and a half hours' — a reverse-engineering contradicted by the source's own stated duration. On his three hours the natural reconstruction is 868 mph x 3 h = 2,604 miles at 33 degrees N, not 1,039 mph x 2.5 h.
findings.fix: In the gloss, quote his own figure: 'after three hours of ascent (his figure; the real ascent was about two and a half)'. In §1, replace the reconstruction with 'Dubay's 2,500 miles is his three hours run at roughly the co-rotation speed; at 33 degrees N and the actual 2.5 h ascent the same reasoning gives 2,169 miles.' Either way the argument is unaffected, and the source stops being misreported.

findings.field: refutation (§2, radiosonde paragraph) and sources[] radiosonde label
findings.problem: The cited Wikipedia radiosonde page says the opposite of what we imply. Its sentence is: '...there may be concern that this could introduce problems into the model initialization. However, this appears not to be so except perhaps locally in jet stream regions in the stratosphere.' We render this as drift 'far enough that the drifting position and time have to be handled in model initialisation, and the article naming that problem singles out jet stream regions as where it bites', and the sources[] label repeats it. We dropped a negation and three hedges ('perhaps', 'locally', 'in the stratosphere') in our own favour, against our own citation — the hedge rule violated on our side.
findings.fix: Keep the verbatim drift quote, which is correct and load-bearing, and drop the assimilation gloss: '...far enough that the same article notes it could in principle disturb model initialisation, though it reports the effect as showing up at most locally, in stratospheric jet-stream regions.' If the stronger claim about drift-aware assimilation is wanted, cite an NWP source that actually makes it.

findings.problem: Internal arithmetic contradiction, in the paragraph the entry itself flags as the one where the rebuttal usually goes wrong. Two sentences apart we write the 43 km lag is 'about one part in a hundred of what the argument requires' and then 'It is wrong by three orders of magnitude'. One part in a hundred is two orders. Reproduced: 42.6 km against 2,169 miles (3,490 km) is a factor of 82.7, i.e. just under two orders on any reading; 43 km against the docstring's own '~4,000 km' is a factor of 93. The docstring carries the same error ('three orders below the ~4,000 km the argument needs'). The overstatement runs in our favour and a defender gets to say we inflated our own margin tenfold and contradicted ourselves in the same paragraph.
findings.fix: Change 'It is wrong by three orders of magnitude' to 'It is wrong by a factor of about eighty' (or 'by nearly two orders of magnitude'), and correct the docstring line to 'two orders below the ~3,500 km the argument needs'.

findings.problem: The Rowbotham search is miscounted and misclassified. We publish: 'Searching the 1865 Earth Not a Globe ... for balloon returns six passages. Five are about the shape of the horizon from the car.' In Project Gutenberg #69892 the word occurs thirteen times (lines 424, 441, 444, 452, 468, 473, 483, 488, 491, 503, 510, 1793, 2900), and the passage at line 1793 is not about horizon shape at all: 'When a balloon sails from an observer without increasing or decreasing its altitude, it appears gradually to approach the horizon' — Rowbotham's perspective explanation of why the Sun appears to ascend and descend. The docstring states the count flatly ('the word "balloon" occurs six times'), so this is not a passages-versus-occurrences quibble. The missed passage is the one that would most strengthen §3: the tradition's founder grounds the same linear-perspective law our sun-angle answer uses, with a balloon.
findings.fix: Rewrite as: 'the word occurs thirteen times: ten in one section on the apparent concavity of the sea seen from the car, one in Rowbotham's perspective explanation of the setting Sun, and one inside a block quotation from the Literary Gazette of 1851.' Then use the perspective passage in section 3: Rowbotham himself explains apparent descent by linear perspective and illustrates it with a balloon, which is the same law that produces converging crepuscular and anticrepuscular rays.

findings.field: passage.gloss ('Nineteen miles a second is the orbit, not the spin') and compression.note (final paragraph)
findings.problem: The 'different target' genealogy claim is over-precise about a source that does not make the distinction. We assert Carpenter's balloon 'is aimed at the Earth's revolution around the Sun' and that ancestor and descendant 'are answering different motions'. Carpenter's own text welds the orbital magnitude to the rotational direction: proof 44 reads 'the Earth is said to move at the rate of nineteen miles in a second of time, "from west to east"', and proof 49 'revolving through space from west to east at the rate of nineteen miles in a second'. He is arguing against 'the motion of the Earth' undifferentiated, using a number that belongs to the orbit and a direction that belongs to the spin. On a project whose product is provenance, attributing a distinction to an author who visibly does not draw it is the wrong kind of tidy.
findings.fix: Replace with: 'Carpenter's number is the orbital one — nineteen miles a second — but he attaches it to a west-to-east direction (proofs 44 and 49), so he is not separating revolution from rotation at all; the modern versions retarget the same picture at the daily spin specifically, at over a thousand miles an hour.' Same finding, no invented precision.

findings.problem: Unscoped absence claim in published prose: 'No physical account says either thing.' That is a claim about an entire literature made from reading two Dubay proofs, and it is the construction the standing rule bans. It sits in straw_man.detail, which the ratcheting test in tests/test_provenance.py does not scan (the loop reads tldr, refutation, untraceable, passage.gloss, compression.note and the cluster note), and in a phrasing none of the _ABSENCE patterns match. This is exactly the batch-8 finding the test's own comment records: writers have learned the regex, not the rule.
findings.fix: Rescope to the texts actually consulted: 'Neither claim corresponds to anything in standard atmospheric dynamics as set out in the thermal-wind and angular-momentum treatments cited here' — or, more simply, state the positive: 'What atmospheric dynamics actually describes is a fluid in near-solid-body rotation with measured departures, and a density profile that falls off smoothly with no boundary to locate.'

findings.field: straw_man.detail ('a rigid co-rotating shell that nobody proposes')
findings.problem: The charge partly misreads its own quotation. Dubay's proof 23, read past the clause we quote, ends: 'It would be spinning around a centre point, therefore the air closer to the ground will always move slower than the air higher up.' That is not a rigid shell being attacked in ignorance — it is a correct statement of what rigid (solid-body) co-rotation implies for linear speed, and it is the premise proof 158 then runs with. Calling it 'a rigid co-rotating shell that nobody proposes' invites the reply that near-solid-body rotation is exactly the zeroth-order model we ourselves defend two paragraphs earlier, so the distinction we are drawing is one of degree (the winds), not of kind.
findings.fix: Narrow the charge to what it can carry: the strawman is 'perfect synchronization' and the abrupt boundary of proof 159, not the altitude-dependent linear speed, which is a correct consequence of the model. Add: 'His own next clause states that consequence correctly; the error is not there but in supposing that a faster absolute speed aloft means motion relative to the ground below.' That also sets up the proof-158 answer the body is missing.

findings.problem: The quotation attributed to proof 21 reads 'If Earth were truly constantly spinning Eastwards at over 1000mph...'. Proof 21 reads 'If the Earth were truly constantly spinning Eastwards at over 1000mph, helicopters and hot-air balloons should be able to simply hover over the surface of the Earth and wait for their destinations to come to them!' It is proof 22 that opens 'If Earth were'. A dropped article is trivial anywhere else; in compression.source_wording, the field whose entire function is verbatim side-by-side comparison, exactness is the point.
findings.fix: Restore 'If the Earth were truly constantly spinning Eastwards at over 1000mph, helicopters and hot-air balloons should be able to simply hover ... and wait for their destinations to come to them!' and note in the locator that the text is Internet Archive OCR (which also renders 1000mph as lOOOmph), so the transcription has not been checked against a printed copy.

findings.problem: The two numbers being compared are computed with different formulas, so the stated ratio is not the ratio of the models. The 13 arcminutes for a Sun 5,000 km up is the elevation-angle shift at a realistic observer geometry (12.1' at 8,000 km downrange, 13.4' maximum, and zero for an overhead Sun) — a small-angle result of order z/2h. The 0.054 arcseconds for the real Sun is z/h, twice the corresponding maximum (0.027"). Computed consistently the two models differ by 1.496e8/5000 = 29,920, not 'about fifteen thousand', and at the same observer geometry by far more. The error is conservative — it understates our own case — but it is an internal inconsistency a checker will find. The same bullets also switch unit systems for the same distances (3,000 miles up and 5,000 miles downrange in one bullet, 5,000 km up and 8,000 km downrange in the next), which reads as an error even though the two pairs are equivalent.
findings.fix: State the geometry once and use it throughout: 'for an observer 8,000 km (5,000 miles) from the point beneath the Sun, rising 39 km moves the Sun's elevation by about 12 arcminutes on the near-Sun model and by under a thousandth of an arcsecond on the real one — the models differ by more than four orders of magnitude.' Pick miles or kilometres for the whole section and give the other in parentheses.

findings.problem: The TLDR says the jet stream's 'direction and roughly 30 m/s speed follow from the Earth's rotation rate'. The body's computation takes two inputs — Omega through f = 2*Omega*sin(phi), and an independently measured pole-to-equator temperature contrast of about 40 K over 5,000 km — and the advocate block's answer to the circularity charge depends specifically on the temperature field being measured separately rather than fitted. Dropping it from the headline gives away, in the first thing a reader sees, the distinction the entry later needs.
findings.fix: '...into a jet stream whose direction and roughly 30 m/s speed follow from the Earth's rotation rate together with a measured pole-to-equator temperature difference.' Eight extra words, and it is the sentence that makes the calculation non-circular.

findings.field: scripts/clusters.py :: A14 originator / originator_work / year / real_source / note (renders inside this entry)
findings.problem: The cluster record contradicts the treatment it renders around. findings.problem: The note asserts that "Artillery stationary calculations" and "Artillery geocentric mils" are both additions the list made — "Neither statement is located in proof 24 of 200 Proofs" — and drift_type="unsourced_addition" is set for the cluster. But the entry itself identifies Hendrie, not Dubay, as the source of the word "artillery", and the test was run only against Dubay. Hendrie p. 112 (verified in the archive OCR) reads: "then the artillery officers and snipers would be trained to consider the spin of the earth in making their calculations for accurate firing. Yet, you will look in vain for any mention of Coriolis effect in any military artillery or sniper instruction manual." Item 114 is a faithful compression of that sentence. So we publish, under the panel heading "The list overstates its own source", a provenance finding that is wrong on one of the two items it names — the mirror image of the sin the hedge rule exists to prevent. (The mils half is sound: I confirmed "mils" occurs 0 times in the OCR of both books.) Secondary: the panel heading reads "The list overstates its own source" while the note's first bolded sentence says the central item does not overstate it.
findings.fix: Split the classification in compression.note and lead with the addition that justifies the panel. Replace the second paragraph's opening with: "Of the other two items, one is an addition and one is not. “Artillery geocentric mils” is the list’s own vocabulary: the word mils is not located anywhere in the archive.org OCR text of either book searched for this entry. “Artillery stationary calculations” is not an addition — it compresses Hendrie at p. 112, where the artillery officers who would be “trained to consider the spin of the earth in making their calculations for accurate firing” are said not to be." Keep drift_type="unsourced_addition" (it is still true of item 407) and let the note carry the split, as the enum is a convenience rather than a theory.

findings.field: refutation, section 2 bullet 2 ("four orders below"); echoed in advocate.best_defense
findings.problem: "Its magnitude is four orders below the effect the claim looks for" is not reproducible from the entry's own numbers. Using the entry's own 155 mm case: the naive model it just described (447 m/s added to and subtracted from a 684 m/s muzzle velocity, range as v^2) gives an eastward range of ~60 km against a westward ~2.6 km, so a predicted east/west difference of ~57 km; the real difference is 2 x 78 m = 156 m. That is a factor of ~370, i.e. 2.6 orders. One-sided it is ~2.9 orders. The only way to reach four is to compare the dimensionless 23:1 ratio against the 0.36% fractional shift, which is not a like-for-like comparison. On a page whose authority rests on arithmetic it computed itself, a headline order-of-magnitude claim overstated by more than a full order is the kind of thing a paid skeptic checks first.
findings.fix: Replace "Its magnitude is four orders below the effect the claim looks for" with a concrete pairing: "The naive version predicts an east/west range difference of tens of kilometres at this range; the real one is about 150 metres — smaller by a factor of several hundred, and still far above what a battery can afford to leave out." Make the same substitution in the advocate's "four orders of magnitude below" so the internal record does not preserve the bad figure.

findings.field: refutation, concession One ("Army artillery doctrine does not use the term"); also section 5 ("the claim has never proposed one")
findings.problem: The first sentence of the concession is correctly scoped — "not located in the text layer of the April 2016 edition ... searched here" — and the next sentence throws the scope away: "Army artillery doctrine does not use the term." That is a universal negative over an entire doctrinal corpus asserted from one document. I ran the project's own lint over this file in isolation: it scores 0 unscoped hits, and the reason is that "not located ... searched here" falls inside the regex's 160-character window and launders the sentence that follows. That is the documented failure mode verbatim — writers have learned the regex, not the rule — and a green ratchet is evidence about the fields it reads and nothing more. Section 5's "and the claim has never proposed one" is the same shape in a field the regex does not pattern-match at all.

clusters.py D17 note is factually wrong and I did not repeat it: 'The Schumann resonance frequency is derived from the Earth-ionosphere cavity treated as a *sphere* of radius 6371 km — the number only comes out right on a globe.' Schumann's ideal formula f_n = (c/2*pi*a)*sqrt(n(n+1)) with a = 6371 km returns 10.59 Hz for n=1, and the observed fundamental is 7.83 Hz — a 26% miss, explained by finite ionospheric conductivity lowering the propagation speed. Suggested replacement: '...treated as a *sphere* of radius 6371 km. The ideal formula gives 10.6 Hz against an observed 7.83 Hz; what matches is the mode ladder, whose ratios are the spherical-harmonic eigenvalue sequence and contain no cavity size.' Also drop 'Sargent's enclosed-world model' from that note when the originator fields are withdrawn.

WHAT THE SOURCE ACTUALLY IS. Our record's originator (Charles K. Johnson, Flat Earth News, 1972) is a hypothesis I could not support with any text. The argument is Victorian and the chain is documented end to end: Rowbotham, Earth Not a Globe (1865) — meridians "converge to the northern centre of the Earth", a mariner steering due west "practically circumnavigates a plane surface … because the earth is a plane" — then Carpenter, One Hundred Proofs (1885), proofs 8–16, the same material cut into numbered one-liners, which is the form this specimen imitates — then Dubay, 200 Proofs (2015), proofs 34–39 and 108–111, which reproduce Rowbotham's own Milner quotation. Passage taken is Carpenter's proof 14 (public domain, quoted in full): parallels of latitude "are circles, which increase, progressively, from the northern centre to the southern circumference … causing the sailor to be continually getting out of his reckoning." The gloss claims an ancestor and nothing more, in the E08 pattern, so it does not contradict the cluster's originator field; the correction is in record_problems.

THE HEDGE RULE, RUNNING BACKWARDS. This is the first argument I have seen where the sources are firmer than the list. Carpenter states his as a flat proof and proof 16 asks for a ratio of 2; Rowbotham stakes a number and asks for a survey. The three list items keep only descriptions true of the globe as well. The refutation therefore answers Carpenter's and Rowbotham's stated predictions, not the fragments — and it opens by conceding the description in the navigator's own manual's words rather than under pressure (Bowditch ch. 24: plane sailing "in which the Earth is regarded as a plane surface"; art. 1524: the celestial sphere is "an imaginary sphere of infinite radius"), keeping the scope sentences adjacent ("to calculate the longitude, the spherical sailings are necessary"; "not intended for distances of more than a few hundred miles").

THE LOAD-BEARING ARGUMENT IS SCALE-FREE. Carpenter supplies the premise: pole at the centre, parallels as concentric circles increasing southward. Grant it and east–west distance per degree of longitude must increase monotonically going south on EVERY north-centred disc, drawn or undrawn. Measured on GRS80 and recomputed for this entry: 111.32 km at the equator, 78.85 km at 45°S, 71.70 km at 50°N. That closes the class of models, not one member, so the "you have refuted Gleason 1892, not us" escape is shut before it opens — which is what the advocate's best defence (rated 4) turns on, and the preemptive instructs future editors not to trim that paragraph down to the punchier azimuthal-equidistant numbers, which do depend on the map.

OTHER RESULTS, all arithmetic reproduced in the docstring. Rowbotham predicted 69.44 statute miles to the degree at 45°S against 45 at 50°N; measured 48.99, so his northern figure is right to about 1% and his southern prediction is 42% high. His 22,000-nmi southern circuit is assembled from sailing routes: the three great circles sum to 14,623 nmi, inside the 15,282 his own table implies — and his figure also overshoots the flat azimuthal-equidistant map's own prediction (16,975 nmi) by 30%, so the Victorian data fit neither model. Modern check anyone can run: Sydney–Perth is published at 3,294 km and about 5 h 15 m, roughly eleven nonstops a day; the same chart puts those airports 8,301 km apart, requiring ~1,580 km/h. Dead reckoning's Southern Ocean errors are directional and locally opposite (Wilkes east of his reckoning, Milner's Cape case west), which no uniform rescaling of southern parallels produces; the ACC is offered as an order of magnitude for one of them and no mechanism is assigned to the other. The gyrocompass answers the "polar navigation" item on its own: Bowditch says its directive force "is maximum at the equator and decreases to zero at the poles" and that its 84-minute period is "the period of oscillation of a pendulum with an arm equal to the radius of the earth" (2π√(R/g) = 84.4 min, recomputed). Grid navigation is used at BOTH poles — "Local Grid North aligns with the Greenwich meridian" at the South Pole — where Carpenter's proof 11 says there is no south point to converge on.

THE SOURCE IS NOT WHO WE SAID. Our record credits Rowbotham 1865; the gunnery vocabulary is not located in that edition. The actual chain is: Tycho → Riccioli/Grimaldi, Almagestum Novum 1651 (arguments 17 and 19 of the 77 — a ball fired toward the pole should be carried off because the ground moves more slowly at higher latitudes) → Dechales 1674 → Dubay, 200 Proofs (2015) proof 24, the east/west cannon claim → Hendrie, The Greatest Lie on Earth (2016) ch. 9, "No Coriolis Effect Proves a Stationary Earth", pp. 105–114, which is where the list's word "artillery" comes from. Sungenis is not involved (no occurrence of artiller-, gunner- or mils in the Vol. II OCR searched).

WHAT DECIDES IT. TC 3-09.81, Field Artillery Manual Cannon Gunnery (HQ Dept of the Army, 13 April 2016 — the same year as Hendrie's book): para 3-63 lists "Rotation of the earth" among deviations from standard conditions affecting both range and deflection; Table H is the range correction by azimuth with a latitude multiplier; Table I is "the correction to deflection in mils, for the rotation of the earth", with tables for every 10° of latitude from 0° to 70° north or south, entered along the top for northern latitudes and "from the bottom" for southern. FM 6-40 (1945) already carries it, taken "for the latitude of the battery (long range weapons only)". Para 7-22's worked theory — gun on the equator firing east impacts over the target, firing west impacts short — is Dubay's proof 24, performed and tabulated.

HEDGE RULE, BOTH CLAUSES. The refutation answers the sources at their own strength and concedes three things in its own voice: the word "Coriolis" is not located in the 2016 artillery manual's searched text (Army doctrine says "rotation of the earth"); it is likewise not located in FM 23-10 Sniper Training (1994), the manual Hendrie's own footnote cites, so his small-arms testimony is true; and the National Geographic passage he attacks is genuinely bad (a great circle on a Mercator projection reported as Coriolis). The kernel is Riccioli's, not Hendrie's, and it is answered on magnitude: his own case (250 paces in 2 s at Bologna) gives a 3–4 cm deflection on guns that scattered by metres, and he explicitly rejected the Copernican "below our ability to measure" reply that was correct. The argument carried its own falsification schedule and lost to longer gun ranges.

ARITHMETIC (recomputed 2026-08-11, cross-checked against the published ~2.8 in for a 1,000-yd northward shot at Sacramento's latitude): D = Ω sinφ·R·T gives 6 mm at 300 m, 7 cm at 1,000 yd, 74 m (3.4 mils) at 22 km, 139 m at 30 km, 1.2 km for the Paris Gun. Eötvös range effect ≈ 78 m (0.36%) for 155 mm at 22 km, against the ~23:1 east/west range ratio the naive 1,000 mph version implies.

Advocate rated 4 — the strongest defence is that "NO ROTATION OF THE EARTH" is a standard condition, so the baseline is a stationary Earth and the tables are fitted fudge factors; and that Table I itself was not read (it is a figure image), only predicted. Both are answered explicitly in the body/preemptive, and the second is stated as an open honesty gap rather than papered over.
